This month is likely to prove an expensive one for many people, for there are more social events this season than last, and with the numerous fetes by which the nation all over the country is evincing its sentiments of loyalty more numerous and daintier frocks than usual are - required. Fortunately for many of , us, fashion does not insist that these toilettes must necessarily be of rich or expen- sive materials, and there are provided many exquisitely pretty fabrics of every imaginable tint and hue which make up into charming dresses and cost only a few pence per yard. Printed muslins are much in demand this year, and the patterns are even more effective than those which caught our fancy last summer. Perhaps the prettiest are those of Pompadour design with quaint garlands of roses, forget- me - nets or other flowers intertwined with knots and twists of ribbon. The ground work is generally covered with small spots, though a few are left plain. It is advisable to choose a Lirs of this style in which the pattern is rather marked, for, as is the case with all delicate tints, the colours are apt to fade a little and become so faint as to be indistinct. I have seen some very pretty coloured muslins of soft yellow, pale heliotrope, pink or blue, but it is not to be gainsaid that these, though sweetly charming at first, when made up lose their colour much more rapidly than those with a white or cream ground printed with a coloured

A PRETTY MUSLIN GOWN. design, A muslin gown is apt to prove some- thing of an undertaking to the home worker, as it requires a certain amount of trimnring and as many frills as the patience of the worker will permit. The charming dress depicted is of figured muslin made in a simple and yet picturesque fashion, such as is considered the height of good taste at present. The skirt in this instance is tucked lengthwise to a little below the knees, where the fulness springs out and finishes in a froth of frills roand the feet. The bodice has a quaint fichu, and the sleeves are of a Turkish order, being very wide and full, and without lining. The yoke is tucked, and the collar and cuffs are of lace and transparent, a little narrow ribbon inter-threaded round the edge matching the pink tones of the flowers with which the gown is patterned, while a twist of pink chiffon finishes the front. There is nothing really so becoming to the fresh beauty of a young English girl as a pretty muslin frock of this style. If the wearer is possessed of a particularly slender waist a sash of rich Chine or brocaded ribbon can be worn, and this looks especially well in company with a pure white muslin frock and a big black hat. The black hat is ever with us, and shows no sign of waning in popular estimation. Indeed, its good qualities are too well known to require pointing out. An all black hat goes with any toilette, whether it be black, white or of gay colouring, while it gives a cachet to a diaphan- ous gown, whether of muslin or lace. These

RE HAT hats are generally of fancy straw, though " crin " lined with tucked chiffon is also fashionable. A charming specimen is given in my sketch. It is trimmed, as indeed most are, with ostrich feathers which are very fluffy at the tips. The new way of trimming a hat with the feathers is to arrange them so that they start at the back of the hat and come round to the front where the tips meet. Sometimes black and white feathers are mingled together, but it is more difficult to achieve success with such a strong contrast, and it is better, I fancy, to keep the hat either all black or all white. The ribs of the feathers are laid back against the crown to produce the ruche - like effect round the front of the brim. Another style of hat which is very fashionable is the tricorne, and this mode looks very rhie when made of soft white tulle in which dainty little pompom roses nestle. A pretty afternoon hat I saw the other day was of burnt straw, the edge being bound with bright red velvet, a line of velvet also being arranged a few inches nearer the face. The brim was trimmed with bunches of bright red cherries and leaves, while a twist of creamy lace and a buckle finished the crown. Another charming hat for the summer wear was one of those becoming constructions of muslin so much in vogue last year. In this case the hat was made entirely of black muslin with only a few poppies to brighten it. A hat of this description is very becoming to a blonde, even more so than the white muslin hats.

The Panama hat threatens to become a nuisance, as its popularity has attained to gigantic propor- tions, and it is to be met with on every side. There are some very horrible imitations of the wnl article which are to be sincerely deplored. It it a mistake to trim a hat of this style elaborately,

far if the plain ribbon band does not satisfy the taste of the wearer a twist of soft ribbon tied at one side in the manner shown in the illustration is sufficient. Flowers are altogether out of keeping, as they destroy the chic simplicity characteristic of this style of hat. Foulard could be substituted for the ribbon if preferred.

There are some very smart cloth dresses with a fine surface being made for summer wear, while coarse oatmeal friezes or canvas in the lightest tones make up very charmingly. The most fashionable of the light colours is termed chainpagne, and this tone looks partieularly well when trimmed and inserted with lace.

The last of the courts at Buckingham Palace was the most brilliant of them all, and the debutaxte who at- tracted the mast attention was Princess Alice of Albany. The Princess is one of the numerous Royal guests who are staying in London for the Ceronation. All the dis- tinguished foreign visitors who have come to this country as guests of the King were also present at the Court, the , Indian Princes alone, constituting a picturesque gather- ing. Whilst, however, the scene inside Buckingham Palace was one of unparalleled splendour, the conditions outside were of a most dreary and gloomy character. The vvaather which has been cold, wet, and wretched on aaela occasion of the five Courts, was at its very worst. so that not even the splendours of toilettes sod tiaras could induce any but a few brave spirits to wait about in the hope of catching a glimpse of their Majesties' guests. The King's -train-bearers at the Coronation are all youthful peers: This is a little contrary to precedent,aii at fermer Coronations they were generally select,ea with- out regard to age. Of the King's train-bearers, the two first, the Earl of Portarlington and Marquis Conyngham, are nineteen years of age, the Earl of Caledon is seven- teen, the Duke of Leinster, and Lord Somers are each fifteen, and Lord Vernon, the youngest, is fourteen. In additicn to the six train-beereis, there are the two pages of honour, Viscount Torrington, and the Don V A Spencer, la-ith of whom are sixteen. The Duke of Leinster is the highest in rank, and of the six young peers selected as train-bearers,four are in the peerage of Ireland.

London is not a beautiful city at any time, and it has been se disfigured by the huge timber structures all along the reute of the Ceronation procession, that visitors frcm the country and abroad can hardly be favourably impressed with the Metropolis. Churches, hospitals, court yards, house fronts, wherever it 'has been possible to erect a stand, or fix a plank, there are these ugly additions, disfiguring many of the most beautiful buildines in London. Most of thesetensporary structures are now ,completed, for which many people are net a littlethankful,lfor what with the hammering, the ladders for fixing illuminations straddling every Ipavement, the t ying shavings and sawdust, it has , scarcely been possible to look up or pass along without suffering from inconvenience. The Coronation has cured many Londoners of the ancient superstition against passing under ladders. So I many have been stretched across the pavements, that pedestrians had perforce to give up all attempts to cir- cumvent them. Many people of course oaly do so in the usual way, to avoid falling paint or other materials, but few of those who acknowledge being superstitious know why it is supposed to be unlucky to pass under ladders. There have been other explanations, but there is no doubt that it originated from the fact that criminals executed at Tyburn had first to past nodes the ladder, in mounting the seaffold. The amazement created by little Jliver Twist, when he ventured to ask for more, could scarcely have exceeded the astonishment of the Commissioners of works, at the request of Mr Cramer, that they would impose regula- tions on the s'ze and shape of the hats which ladies may wear in Palace Yard on the occasion of the Coronation. Men who have suffered from the- matieee hat will be disposed to sympathise with Mr Crenser in Mils matter, but it is perhaps scarcely to be wondered at that the Commissioners should decline to undertake the task. Mr Akers-Douglas hss bad some experience as a Parlia- mentary whip, of bringing pressure to bear upon men, but the exercise of even a mild coercion upon women is, he evidently thinks, quite another question. It is to be trusted, however, that women who intend 'to occupy seats where it will befoossible for their head- gear to obstruct the view of others, will carefully con- sider the subject. The neat small toque—minus trimming —that throws a little shade over the eyes in case the sun should shine, and which the downpours we are now vers tamilar with could not spoil, i undoubtedly the mod sensible and considerate of headgear for all occupying outside seate. The Coronation rap, which some millin- ers have been endeavouring to brim, into favcur.is much less desirable from every point of view. There will be a great variety of muslins, and the lighter dress materials offered at the Summer sales which commence on ;lune 30. As a rule, these facilities for shoppinrat sacrificial prices, commence on the first Monday in July, hut they have no doubt been hurried forward tg catch the coronation visitore—great will be the scramble, and the bargains in summer fabrics ought to beat'the record. There have been so few opportuni- ties for wearing light costumes that there must be largo stocks of the lighter summer materials to dispose of. and judicious purchases will no doubt become useful later on. Some people are convinced that there is to be little or no summer this year. They have been look- ing up the precedents which they say point te I his eon- elusion, but there iereally nothing new in our arriving at Midsummer Day without any summer. Walpole I wrote in the middle of June 1768, that the only sunshine that was any good to him was made from Newcastle I oral, sod ttat while the poets talk of shady grow, and II pleasant breezes, peaple sat at home with sore throats and the ague.

Our long spell of national meurning'taught us:that the combination of black and white is invariably becoming, and much less costly than colours. But collectively it is distinctly depressing, and one welcomes. in an !Ulf OM- bly where black and white gowns predominate (as thev almost always do) individuals who have taken their courage in their hands, and garbed themselves in bright hues. Possibly the weather has bad much to do.with the continued popularity of the black and white'scheme an. has little heart to don one's cheery looking frocks, under leaden skies and persistent downr ours. Sashes in varied ferms have long ban in high favour, but the lace sash is quite the newest variety and gives a delightful finiil to a muslin, tulle, chiffon, or other .1 light fabric " gown. In more ways than one, the sash Is a boon and • blessing to womenkind. To begin with, it is most becoming, it bides the sometimes not altogether successful fastenings of the skirt band, and moreover covers the creased and crushed appearance of the back breadths of a middle aged gown, as it ficere gracefuly to the lortr.

"Au revoir, captain," he said, "I understand; but I have to keep an appointment, in spite of the rain; I will certainly do what you ask; while I am as inquisitive as a magpie about your widow, I will be as mute as a. mole. Adieu."

He darted down the steps like a boy, while the captain shrugged his shoulders, and wondered how any man could be such a fool as to risk a wetting for the sake of a woman; he guessed that this rush through the rain was for the sake of Mademoiselle Sophie. "We must manage to save Loigerot from this adventuress," he thought, as he stared at the steady down-ponr, and wished for an umbrella, "he is the best fellow I know, and the most likely to be imposed on. He thinks women angels." " H—h—m" sounded close to him.

The captain started from his meditation as though he had been struck, and turned round; the voice had seemed to come from behind him; there stood the beggar. She had risen from her chair, and she stood facing him, her knotted hands clasped on a stick. His surprise at first kept him silent. He stood staring at her. Her face impressed him, it was so full of power, and also of suffering ; the sightless eyes were closed, and receded deeply under her straight black brows; her forehead was pale and strongly lined, while close together at the begin- ning of each eyebrow, were two yet deeper lined that told of martyrdom to pain ; the woman's face was so thin, that the cheeks seemed to be drawn together, and a faint streak of colour showed on them; her lips were almost colourless, but het nose was singularly handsome, large and well. formed.

"Did you speak, my good woman?" he s:dd, when he had finished his survey. He put his hand in his pocket as be spoke. The woman shook her head, and knocked her stick on the stone pavement in protest. . . .
"Pardon me, monsieur," he thought her voice was very gentle, "I am only asking foil' your attention; I can give Monsieur the information he seeks for, if he will have the patience to listen tr. me."
Guiney looked amused, but he felt puzzled: "Tell away, my good woman, I am all atten- tion."

"If monsieur will have the goodness to come and stand by me, I will go back to my chair. I. am only, Monsieur sees, a poor cripple, and I shall tell my story better it I sit. Guiney smiled with increasing amusement, but he felt compassionate, and to his own surprfse he put out his hand to help the woman back to her chair. She, however, managed to reach it unaided.
" I thank monsieur," she said, and then slowly, and with evident pain she resumed her usual stooping position "Monsieur has been speaking of the Lieutenant LOigerot ; he is a friend of his . .

Captain Guiney -had beard from his comrades queer tales about the wonderful wisdom of the blind beggar of St. Maclou ; he had laughed at them as he laughed at everything else but now he straightened himself, and looked keenly at his companion to make sure that she was really blind. "Yea, my good woman Monsieur Loigerot is my friend; what have you tc, say about him?" "Nothing about him, Monsieur, except that he is good and generous; he is also'my friend; I have to speak of the lady he walks about with, the lady he escorted last Sunday to La Pouille." _

"The devil" the captain exclaimed, "how can you know that Monsieur Loigerot went to La Pouille?" he added mildly. She smiled very sadly. "At your age, Monsieur, you will have learned that there is much going on in life of which we are all ignorant; at my age I tell you to leave this undercurrent undisturbed; I will tell you all I can to help your friend, and you may believe me, but the way in which I know this truth is, pardon me, Monsieur, simply my own affair." He stared at the blind woman in increasing sur- prise; he judged from her way of speaking that she was an educated person, and he felt very curious to know how she had been dragged down to her pre- sent position; he saw however that questions would be useless and out-of-place. "I accept your conditions, friend; tell me what you know of this lady, and I shall be thankful; you are sure," he said severely, for he began to think that, after all he might be imposed upon, "you are sure that you really know who Madame Jamain is, for I must sift this matter to the bottom."'

The woman's lip curled. "She is not Madame Jamain, monsieur, she is not a widow; she is a single woman; her real name is Juliette Carron. Do I know her, you ask? I knew her well, monsieur, all her life till she left her home ; since then she has had a child, a son who must be at least twenty years old by now." "Ma foi " the captain exclaimed, "a son of twenty I It cannot be, for I saw this lady last night at the theatre, she looked young and beautiful."

"I should have thought," the beggar said slowly, "that you, Monsieur, would have been clearer- sighted than your friend." Her sarcasm brought the colour to his face. "You mean that this lady is not so young as she looks—that she is too old for my friend.." "I mean more than that, Monsieur; but you shall have proof of what I say; I do not want to bring trouble on this—this—lady; I want you to hinder trickery, Monsieur, but I chiefly, wish to save your friend, and I can give you the means, 4j_ you will take them. Not far from here, in the - Rue du Doight, you will find at the corner of an alley a small Cafe. Go in, Monsieur, and look round you, you are almost sure to see a young fellr, I fancy about the age of your friend; that is young Gustave Carron; he has but lately Mimi to Rouen, and he spends most of his time at this Cafe, drinking; he will tell you as he has told others, about the grand future in store for him, when his mother shall have become Madame Loigerot." "Is this true ? " Captain Guiney frowned heavily as he spoke. "Every word of it, Monsieur ; you are wonder- ing why I tell you this? I who seem to have more in common with this mother and her drunken son, than with a brave young officer? Monsieur, I will tell you why Ido it. It is because in all the weary years I have sat here, so changed that no one who knew me in my better days could recognise me, not one soul of the many passers-by has ever spoken to me as your friend has spoken; he has made me feel that I am not to him the miserable degraded beggar I appear to the rest; he speaks to me as to a fellow-creature, and a friend. Adieu, Monsieur, I have told you enough to serve your purpose; it has left off raining, and you can go your way." She muffled her face in her shawl, and Guiney felt that he was dismissed.
"Thank you, my friend, I am very much obliged to you ; " he dropped a coin in her box, and hurried down the steps, on his way to the cafe in the Rue du Doight.

THE BLIND BEGGAR,
BY KATHARINE S. MACQUOID, (Author of "Patty," " AppledoreFarm," &c.)

div.head: PART IL -CHAPTER lll—Continued.
div.p: PART IL -CHAPTER lll—Continued.
CHAPTER IV.

Loigerot stood before Madame Jamain's door considering; his excitement calmed down, and he determined to do nothing in a hurry, Madame was as dear to him as ever, but his anticipations had lost some of their brightness; finally, he decided not .to propose to-day, unless his beloved could give a satisfactory account of her acquaint- ance with this ypung man; he saw, too, that it might be difficult to question Madame Jamain. He was shown into a smart little room upstairs, and his hostess received him very graciously; she gave him rapturous thanks for his gift, and looked for several minutes admiringly at the dainty blue satin box, but, when she lifted the lid, she gave a little cry of delight which enchanted the lieutenant; she then proceeded to taste first one and then another of the exquisitely arranged sweets, while she declared each one was better than the other. Madame Jamain saw that her admirer was ill at ease, and she was anxious he should recover his self-possession; she felt sure he had come to propose to her, and though it was early in their acquaintance, there were cogent reasons against delay; therefore, after a little more dallying with ,the sweetmeats, she half-closed the pretty box, and proceeded to give her admirer an opening. "I believe, monsieur, that you are not a native of this part of the country?" she said, sweetly. "Pardon me, madame, I come from farther north. I was born in the neighbourhood of St. Omer; and—aw—you, madame, may I ask what part of France had the honour of giving you birth?"

"Never mind that honour now," she smiled with engaging playfulness, "I am so interested in pursuing my inquiriqs about you, that it bores me to turn aside to speak of myself; you will pardon me the abruptness of my question, but I heard that you came from Strasbourg in Alsace, and I used to have friends there with whom you may be possibly acquainted. Ah I I forget that you are a native of Picardy." The lieutenant swelled with conscious pride. Here was the chance he had longed for ever since he had thought of marrying Madame Jamain, the chance of announcing that he was a landholder. _„ " Midame," he slowly puffed out his wordsl& if they were whiffs from a pipe, " I—aw—am, it is true, Picard by birth, and yet, by the rights o: my position, I—aw—am Alsatian, although, strange to say, I have never beenin Alsace." Madame Jamain looked surprised. "How is that?" she said, softly, and he fancied her blue eyes were full of interest and curiosity, "sweetly heLtold himself. "Madame, I—aw possess a small property there; for the present it is managed by the very respectable tenant to whom I let it yearly; so that Madame—l—aw—" he looked at her, and began to stammer; he all at once remembered his resolution, and he meant to keep it; "whenever I retire from the service, Madame, I have a borne, and also a pursuit waiting for me, in the—aw—the cultivation of my property. He paused, surprised at his own flow of words. _ _

"Yes, yes, Monsieur, I see," here she coughed, with a_ little smile that seemed to say, "1 am listening." Loigerot had taken courage. He said suddenly: "May I, without presumption, Madame, ask you the name of that gentleman, with whom you were talking yesterday, at—" He was interrupted by a shriek from Madame Jamain. The lovely blue casket had slipped off the table, it lay on the floor, its sugared contents being scattered over the carpet. " Heavens ! what is to be done ? " Madame cried, clasping her white hands; "I must ring for a spoon." Loigerot had flung himself on his knees, and had already collected a handful of sugar-plums; but at this he looked up in some alarm, and then gaged at his brown fingers—to which the bon-bons were tenaciously clinging—as if they had committed saarilecre. Madame Jamain looked round. She saw the sweets scattered all over the floor, while Loigerot sprawled in the midst of them, his face grotesque with dismay; she could not help it, she sank back in her chair and laughed till she cried. Loigerot rose instantly to his feet, frowning a little, as he scrambled himself erect, then he glanced at his trousers to see if they were free of sugar-plums. " I—aw—will not venture, Madame, to offer you any further assistance, but if you will permit me, I—aw—will give myself the pleasure of bringing you--aw—to-morrow another box of bon-bons. ' He bowed with some dignity, for he was morti- fied that Madame Jamain could laugh at such a misfortune. '

"Pardon me, dear Monsieur, I ought not to laugh, but I still feel sometimes like a school-girl. You will forgive me, will you not!" He saw tears in her blue eyes, as he boa ed over the hand she held out.

"How good and generous you are, dear Monsieur Loigerot," she said tenderly. She gently pressed his hand, and the sweetness of her glance quenched the remains of his anger. They had a little more talk, and then he loft her.
"Sweet angel," he said to himself, as he went down the not very clean staircase, ".1 believe slat loves me; she shall have a bigger box."

The brilliant weather suddenly clouded over, . and as Captain Guiney and Lieutenant La Peyre, coming from different points, neared the church of St. Maclou, there came down such a torrent of rain that the two officers instinctively hurried up the steps and sheltered themselves in the porch. The blind beggar was sitting there as usual. At the sound of the pathetic chink—chink, the cap- tain dropped a few centimes into the tin box. The woman thanked him. She was muffled in a shawl this morning which hid her face. She seemed to be very old and infirm as she bent over her money-box. • "You are just the man I want, La Peyre," the captain said, "this shower gives you time to listen to me ;" this with a sarcastic smile' for his comrades said that La Peyre devoted every moment he could spare to the society of Made- moiselle_Devisme.

" With the greatest pleasure,"—honest La Peyrs smiled and stood ready to listen. The captain glanced at the beggar; she sat srouched together, he fancied she was asleep. "Well, I want to talk to you about Loigerot ; he is running himself into a net with his widow, and he may find it hard to get free." "Why do you not warn him, Captain? He is your friend. La Peyre had never been singled out by his cap. tam n as Loigerot had; he therefore felt surprised, oven shocked, that Captain Gainey should discuss his special friend with a third person. "My good fellow,"—again there was a sarcastic tone in the Captain's voice,—"excuse me but this is a question of the heart, and I—l believe that one's friends are apt to become deaf to advice on such a subject. Understand me, La Peyre, I do not ask you to persuade our friend to open his eyes, he would only close them more resolutely. Neither shall I speak to him myself; I cannot afford to wound my friend Loigerop, No, you have not caught my drift." He put his head on one side, and looked at the young fellow with half-closed eyes. He was cal- culating the moonlit, ot 1,0,1 which La Peyre was likely to afford in too ULU toLoa. "Then what do you want, Captain?" La Peyre said bluntly. Captain Guiney slightly shrugged his shoulders. He thought: "This good fellow's perception is as tough as the hide of a jackass." "My good friend," he said, "I think you already know a good many people in Rouen; I want you to spend a little time in making enquiries for me; I want to know something about Madame domain ; about her late husband, and her former place of residence. lam told she has not been long here. I also wish to know who are her associates and acquaintances; I feel uneasy about her. I shuu matte enquiry on my side. It will be bard if between us we do ;tot unearth some facts which may open the eyes of our friend; but we must ho absolreakty cautious, we must not give any alarm; and we must let facts speak for themselves; Loigerot may be hard to convince, but if there ever lived an honest, upright man, it is Loigerot— he is not to be moved by mere •assertions, re- member."
La Peyre laughed. "Honest," he said, in a loud voice, "yes, we all know that Loigerot is honest, but he is as obstinate as a mule." The in h 4 spoken in a low

div.head: CHAPTER V.
div.p: CHAPTER V.

Five of the officers of the 75th regiment break- fasted together at the Hotel de France; among these five were Captain Gainey and Lieutenant Loigerot. After breakfast this morning, the Captain asked Loigerot if he would call for him in the afternoon. _ _

"I want you to do me a favour," he said, and while his friend chuckled with delight, the captain added, "I wish you would take me with you to call on your friend, Madame Jamain. I saw the lady with you at the theatre on Wednesday, and I am anxious to make your acquaintance; she certainly does credit to your taste, you sly dog." Loigerot beamed with delight, but he hesitated; it seemed to him that the proper course would be first to ask Madame Jamain 's permission to present his friend, and he said so. Guiney, heiwever, over- ruled this objection, he was so enthusiastic in his admiration of the beauty of his friend's choice while he assured him that this presentation would be entirely en regle, that Loigerot consented to call for the Captain and gave himself up to the satisfaction he should enjoy in introducing his distinguished friend to his beautiful idol. 'She must astonish and satisfy even his critical taste," he told himself. He went to the flower-shop in the Rue Jeannee d' Arc and ordered a lovely bouquet to be sent to Madame Jamain; it would be delightful, he thought, to find her admiring his flowers; and then he waited impatiently till the time fixed by the Captain arrived. Loigerot was silent and absorbed as they walked along; he told himself he was a coward. Why had he not succeeded in getting an answer from his idol on the subject of her disreputable acquaint- ance. He had not even repeated his question; he had gone to see her on the following day with a still larger box of bon-bons, and had been told that Madame was engaged with the hairdresser; the maid, however, presented him with a tiny scented note, which saiu that Madame Jamain had taken a box at the theatre that evening, and hoped that Mon- sieur Loizerot would eisoorkiher, She had looked

so rovefrin evening rci—ei-W-Miit- the young soldier fairly lost his head, and forgot all about his important question until next morning. He had meant to ask it this afternoon, and now Gtiney's presence would make it impossible. The Captain was also lost in thought: it was difficult to plan his attack until he had seen his friend's enchantress.

They reached the top of the narrow stairs, and were announced. Loigerot was delighted when ke saw in Guiney's eyes the admiration his friend felt at sight of the charming widow. He thought, too, that he had never seen his friend so pleasant, so courteous and talkative; Gniney was evidently determined to make himself agreeable, and the ease of his friend's manner set the young lover himself at his ease. His charming Juliette was at first more silent than usual, but as soon as her reserve melted she smiled, and seemed to enjoy the Cap- tain's rather broad compliments. LOigerat brimmed over with happiness, Madame Jamain had never seen him in such gay spirits. They talked about the theatre, and both his companions laughed at Loigerot's jokes about the incidents of the evening. For some time the flow of talk and laughter was incessant.

In the midst of it, without waiting for a pause of opportunity, Captain Guiney said in the same pleasant careless tone: "What a tall fellow your son is, Madame; I am fortunate enough to have the pleasure of his acquaintance." Loigerot was thunderstruck; he glanced at his Juliette, and grew pale at what he saw; her face was dark, and convulsed; he was furious with Guiney. How could he be so careless; he had made some mistake, and given this sweet creature the greatest pain. He saw that she was now frowning. He looked angrily at Guiney. "Monsieur le Capitaine," he began. but Madame broke in and interrupted him: "My son! Heavens I how droll !" She smoothed her frown away, and laughed out as she looked at Guiney. "Pardon me, Madame,"—the Captain laid aside the flowery courtesy he had hitherto used, and spoke sternly—" there is no possible mistake on my part. I had a talk with your son yesterday, and again to-day, and I am determined to caution you in regard to his habits. Madame, he drinks too much, and he is too fond of play. He will ruin both you and himself. He tells me you are so devoted to him, that you are going to sacrifice yourself to pay his debts, you are going to marry so that your son may have funds for the future." Madame sat silent, she was pale, and she bit her lips. Presently she said: "I can only repeat that Monsieur is mistaken. He had better in future be more correct in his information when he attacks a defenceless woman, for it seems to me that I am defenceless against insult." She glanced contemptuously at Loigerot. He had risen, and even through the bronze of his weather-beaten skin, he changed colour._

His first idea wes'to restot; peace. He was not quick-witted enough to see the meaning of the Cap. tam's words; it had been a great shock to learn that this adorable woman had a child, but as he listened attehtively, his friend's changed manner impressed him; he did not remember that Guiney had said any- thing rude; Loigerot began to see thatthe Captain had only meant to caution this devoted mother against her boy's bad habits; he was doubtless some precocious little schoolboy. If Guiney would only go away, he thought, he could soon soothe his Juliette into her usual sweet smiling mood. Loigerot coughed and looked at his friend, but the Captain seemed unconscious of his uneasiness ; Guiney leaned back in his chair, his eyes were fixed en Madame Jamain.

" Pard,on me," he said, "I do not wish to paM you more than I can help, but I must ask why you call yourself Madame Jamain when your eon's name is Carron? Also I must ask why your son's existence is to be kept secret from my friend Lieutenant Loigerot ? Your son told me this him- self."

"-I am Willing," she said, "to offer any explana- tion that the Lieutenant may delire ; but Ido not feel called on to explain my private affairs to you, Monsieur. Why should I?" she said, with such calm insolence that Guiney felt irritated. He rose from his chair; he had been unwilling to de#ert his friend, but he thought that Loigerot's eyes must now be fully opened, and that his own good sense would save him from this adventuress.

"Good day, I will leave you to explain," he said cavalierly. There was silence in the room, while the clank of the captain's footsteps sounded on I the stairs. Madame waited in the hope that Loigerot would apologise for his friend's behaviour, but when his silence Continued, her anger broke bounds; she hid her face in her handkerchief and sobbed hysteri- cally. /

Loigerot was distracted; he walked up and down the room cursing himself for a fool; why had hi not let things be? Why had he consented to bring that cynic, Guiney,.to trouble his happiness? He looked at his Julietta ; her fair face was hidden in her handkerchief, while her shoulders heaved with convulsive sobs. Loigerot had never seen a woman in such an agony of sorrow, and his tender heart carried him beyond all prudence. He put his arm round her, and kissed her fair perfumed hair.
She looked round at him, full of anger. "Come, come, dearest," he said tenderly, "You are not angry with me, are you?" _ .
She tho—ught he was at her mercy, and she resolved not to explain;. she would make him feel that he was to blame.

44 I es, ..he said gravely, "I am very angry with you for not being angry • how could you bring that scoundrel to see me, andinsult me? It is infamous. How can you be friends with such a liar? You should have made him swallow his base false- . hoods." ' Her eyes shone with anger, as she drew herself away; he could not see a trace of tears. "Pardon me, Madame," he spoke stiffly, "my friend is a man of honour; he may be mistaken, but for all that he is my friend."
She looked scornfully as she shrugged her shoulders.

"Mon Dieu! Is that your opinion? I am not to be angry, because he is your friend. I am to listen calmly while he blackens my child, my dear little boy, and because he is tall for his age, credits him with the vices of manhood, the sweet innocent. Cinaille ! If I were a man I would soon stop his mouth." She again put her handkerchief to her eyes. Her last words disturbed Loigerot. When Gainey first spoke of Juliette's son, the lieutenant had remembered the young fellow he had twice seen and about whom he had questioned Madame Jamain; .he had been too much upset and taken by surprise fully to .grasp his friend's meaning, now the captain's words suddenly came back to him; it may be that Madame's words had jarred his sensi- bility ; why did she talk of a child; a child would not speak as Guiney said you Carron had spoken. He paused. Guiney had asked why the son's name was different? Loigerot grew cold as he recalled the Captain's manner.

He was freed from the spell of those lovely eyes; his Juliette had turned away; he felt that he had a right to ask questions. "Excuse me, Madame," he said, "but have I not also a grievance ?" She noted his changed tone. Looking round, she smiled at him. "Tell me dear friend what is it ?"

But Loigerot did not look at hei.- " You have been strangely silent about your— aw—child, Madame. May I ask why he is called Carron?" he said stiffly. "You may ask, dear friend," she laughed merrily, "but I cannot auswer you, that is a family secret. Now be reasonable, sit down I coMmand you." She looked at him languishingly, but Loigerot stood almost more upright than usual, while he pulled fiercely at his moustaches, then he walked up and down the room. "Great Heavens, Madame," he said at last, "I do believe you have lied to me all through. Madame," he vent on with increasing severity, as he stood looking down on her, "I see plain at last, I understand it all; it was your son I saw at La Pouille. I have seen him leaving this house. Madame, you have deeply wronged me, you have done worse than you meant to do; you meant to plunder a credulous young solider, but you have done far worse; you have destroyed my faith in woman for many a year to come. Adieu, Madame."
She caught at his arm, "My Achille," she said softly, "I will explain—" He shoek her off roughly, "It is too late." Then with very unusual dignity, he walked out of the doom. TIIE END.

After three hours' discussion on Tuesday, the Lon Con County Council unanimously decided to seek for powers in the next session of Parliament to acquire, tabe over, and administer the river piers and tanning stages on the Thames, to construct additional piers and alter the loca- tion of the piers from time to time, and to establish an efficient steamboat service on the river. The Council decided to purchase the Marble Hill estate, Twickenham, so as to preserve the view from Richmond Hill.

div.p: THE THIRD CONTINGENI OF VvARRINC3TON VOLUNTEERS.
Home Again Next Week.

Next week Warrington will not only witness the Coronation celebrations but also the home coming ot the third contingent of Warrington Volunteers. The War Office, announced on -.Nicnday night that Captain B Fairclough and 25 men bad embarked at Durban on the s.s Syria, and were due to arrive at Southampton on the 25th or 26th of this month. From this announcement it is not quite clear whether any of the men will be home in time to take part in the local festivities, but it is to be hoped that they will at least witness some parL, of them. _ _ _
The men, whom Warrington will welcome home next week sailed from Southampton for South Africa on the 6th of April last year, so that they have been absent on active service a little over 15 months.

The following composed the contingent when it left Warrington : Captain B Fairclough Sergeant C I Thornley, 10, Porter-street Corporal J Sewell, 49, Legh-street Bugler J Bramell, 27, .Faircloueb's-avenue Lance-Corporal W Green, 66, Regent-street, Earlestown Private C Blackburn, 17, Glasshouse-row „ T Bird, 236, Manshester-road „ J Burrows. 17,Dudley-street „ E Clarke, 4, Heaton-street „ A J Crozier, 37, Lythgoes-lane „ J H Dutton, 8, Blue Coat-street „ W Davies,ls, Wellington-street „ M Walsh, 5, York-street • M Foster, 19. Death has removed Private Arthur Richardson, whe diel at Heidelburgt, on May 17th last year, from dysentry. Private Woodhead has been invalided home, and four others have been left behind. THE EDUCATION BILL. ---- The Rev F A Screeton and Religious _ .
Education.

The Rev F A Screeton, Vicar of Christ Church, Latch- ford, preached at St Barnabas' Church on Sunday even ing, when the concluding service in connection with the patronal festival was held. The offertory was on behalf of the Day and Sunday School funds. The preacher selected for his text the words " Take tais child and nurse it for me," and, in the course of his sermon, said that in the eventful and hazardous interval between

childhood and manhood or womanhood, there were two terrible powers of evil to be met with—ignorance and sin—and a true education was one which would enable a child to combat these two powers and to overcome them Education was only mis-called educatioe, and only half did its work unless it dealt with character as well as with intellect', with the heart and be mild as well as aide merely the brain. True education mint deal with not just one part of a human being, but it must deal with the whole—with the body, eeul and spirit. It must make children straight, honest, brave and self-reliant men and women. It must not merely sharpen their wits, because by doing that it might make them cleverer rogues ; it must not convert their brains into a sort of portmanteau into which could be crammed as many facts as possible about geography, arithmetic, and so forth. True education must strengthen and mould the character, develop the whole being, and open the eyes of the children to the high calling of duty to God and to man. No education, he ventured to say, was complete, and no education was capable of making children good and useful citizens which did not develop their moral nature, and which did not induce them to do what was right and to love it because it was right, and to avoid what was wrong because it was wrong. That was true education and he knew of RO power in the world which could help them to do this so splendidly as the power of the Christian religion. The rev gentleman went on to speak in favour of the combination of relig- ious and secular education. If they gave children a God- less roducatian, an education merely secular, they (the children) would sooner or later be like a frail ship sent rudderless en a stormy sea with a broken compass pointing inlno definite direction,andthey would turn their arithmetic into roguery and their literature into lusteEducation must be inspired and animated by the spirit of religion if it was to do good. Thirty years ago a great education bill was passed which provided that every child in this country should be brought up as an educated child. It was confidently prophesied by people who were very anxious to have that Bill passed that, when everybody was educated the publichouses had to cease to temnt, and it was said that increased edncation would drive out the demons' of lust and immorality. "Look" they said "at our prisons. They are fulrof people and two-thirds of them can neither readlnor write. " Theyiseemedto say "Only teach them, and educate them, and we shall need no prisons, and no publichoueen" Had that been so ? Every child in the country for the last thirty two years had been educated. Was there leas crime? Were there no prisons ? Were there no pubfichousos ? The prisons were full to-day - and the only difference between the prisoners thirty- two years ago and at the present time was that thirty two years ago two-thirds of them could not read and write and now two-thirds of them could read and write. Did not this go to prove that mere secular educa- tion, not inspired and animated by the Christian religion, would not save children from evil and would not make them into honest men and women ? A mere secular education was too likely to produce large brains and little hearte, and that was not what they wanted to produce. He heard of people complaining that the clergy of the Church of England were opposed to the people being enlightened and educated. There were some foolish people who talked like that, but surely the clergy could be acquitted. The clergy were anxiouiefor the people to be educated, and, more than that, the Church of England was the I first body in the country to start the process of (dime- , tin. The Church of England planted a day school in , every parish in England before anybody else thought of doing anything in the work of education at all. If the English people were to hold supremacy in the commer- eial ' world they must be an educated people, and no money which was spent on education was a bed invest- meat. It was a good investment and a sound national investment. Indeed, he did net thiek we bad done enough in the matter of education. A great percentage of children left school now when they wereunder fourteen. While children in Germany were going on having their intelligence expanded, a great many English children in large towns were turned out to work in factories, Sze. The preacher,continuing,said the one chiefldesign of the Bill which was now before Parliament was to give relief to the Church voluntary schools. They found that in the exigencies of present circumstances!, when the cost of education was becoming larger and larger every year, it was impossible by voluntary means to keep the schools up to the standard that they would like them to be kept unto, and so the object of the Bill was to enable them to maintain the schools out of the rates,though the maintenance of the fabric of the schools would still depend upon them (the Church people). If Church people wanted a new school anywhere, and they could get permission to build it, they would have to pay for It out of their own pockets. On the other hand, if people wanted an undeaominational Reim' in any particular district—even if there was a Church school— they could have it, and it would be provided out of the rates. He did not think, so fir as Chisrch people were concerned. that the Bill unduly favoured them. In towns where there were two systems of education— Church schools and unoenotninetional or Board schools —Church people would not only have to pay the erdin ary rates but they would have to maintain the fabric of- the Ceurele schools and nay for new schools if they wanted them, whilst all the :ether schools would be maintained and built out of the rates. And yet, curi- ously enough, how some people were shrieking over this 1 Education Rill, and saying such hard things about the 1 clergy, as if they (the clergy) were going to line their pockets with gold out of this Bill. They might say all ' these hard things if it were a sort of contract let out to them (the clergy) by which they were going to mako some • fortune. But it was not so. It was simply that the Church schools would be onebled by the rates to maintain their position and to give a good education to the children who attended them. Speaking of the "religious diffi- culty " the preacher said it was a difficulty on platforms and in pulpits hut it was not a difficulty any where else. It was net a difficulty in the schools, for the parents who sent their children re Church 'schools know perfectly well that the church people did not try to mike Baptist children into Church children, nor Wesleyan children into Church children. They made no attempt to do 80, and the statement that they did was absolutely false. rise-me who knew: anything about the schools and who over went into them, would know that a statement like that wee abeolutely contrary to the fens. He had never known in his experience—and he had been a manager of Church scesols for about thirteea years—% single Dissenting ehild in Church scksols become a Churchman or Churchwoman becanee they went to a Churc'a day school. Where was the religious difficulty ? They did on one morning in the week teach the Church Catechism and if this was a hardship, there was the conscience clause, and people who did not approve of that could keep their children dial away from that religious instruction, ask the teacher at the day school to provide some other and that would be dons Why all this noise ? Why all those hard thicgs said about the clergy P The schools instead of being a Ince ativeinvestment to the clergy cost them a tromendeus amount of timejanxiety, and money. There were now two ways fie which they could deal with the religious difficulty, and that was either to give no religious in- struction in the day schools at all or, if people felt so strongly about it, to allow the Free Churches to appoint someone to go into the schools and teach their own chil- dren. The latter would be a plan which they (Church people) would approve of and to which they would sub- mit. It we; actually proposed by the Archbishop of Canterbury that that arrangement should be made, but unfortunately their Nonconformist friends, fer whom he had the greatest respect,would not hear of this arrange- ment. Yet,that scheme could be carried out if only they meant to get ever the difficulty. If only people would be reasonable, and if on the subject of religion, about which they all ought to be full of love, they did not loss their heads and get very angry, but tried to understand 1 one another instead of saying hard words, they would get over a difficulty like that very easily indeed. He I did not think there was one person in a thousand who would want no religious instruction at all in the schools. They could not leave religions instruction merely to the Sunday School. An hour in a Sunday School on Sunday was not going to make up for instruction given by trained and disciplined teachers every day of the week. It could not snake up for it. If religious teaching was excluded from the day schools it would also imply a divorce of religion from everyday life and they ought not to divorce religion from every- day life. He thought the proposal to do so was one which the people of England would not submit to. The members of the Church of England had a perfect .right to demand that the religious instruction for their children should be the teaching of the Church of England. The other kind of teaching which obtained in the Beard schools, and which was called undenominationaliem, satisfied one class of the com- munity. It satisfied, the Nonconformists—he was not saying anytismg disrespectful of them—and vet Church
Once there was no soap in the world, and washing was very hard work. Soap eased it.
Then came Fels-Naptha and eased it again as much more. It is the money-back soap. 21-cl a bar. Fels-Naptha soap Peninsular House Monument London E C

people were obliged to provide that out of the rates. People who lived in Board school towne paid the rates and paid for that instruction, although as Church people they did not approve of it. Church people said that Church instruction ought to be provided for Church children is Church schools. Was that an unreasonable demand ? Church people paid rates and taxes like other people. They paid perhaps a greater proportion of rates and taxes than any other elass. If that be 80 he eontended they were right in demandiag that Church teaching should be given in Church day schools, at any rato for Church children.

div.head: PROTESTING AGAINST THE EDUCATION BILL.
div.p: PROTESTING AGAINST THE EDUCATION BILL.
Sir John T. Brunner M.P. Visits 'Runcorn. u.

Oa Monday evening,a public meeting was held,at,Run- corn ,under the presidency fof Mr F J Norman for I the purpose of protesting :against the Government Bill. Oa the platform were Sir John T Brunner,Bert,M.P.,fMr Ellis Griffiths,M.P.,the Revs J Osberne,l B Foster and W Eyre, Messrs S Taylor, A R Norman, J R Fritb,R H Poenett, G Bellamy, W Handley, J M Frith and others. Sir John T Brunner, in an energetic speech, said that they had now reached a definite turning point in their national history. There was before them a most deter- mined fight which would never end, except with one result, between the forces of priestly ascendency and the forces of democratic power. This contention was directly attributable to the death of Mr Gladstone. The empire coald only remain great by upholding the principles of liberty. If resistance were hopeless to the Bill they would still endeavour to introduce improvements into it founded on Liberal principles. Iv was wrong to allow or to claim irresponsible power. And therefore on that point the Bill had his most sturdy opposition. The offence in the Bill was its manifest desire for non-progress. The Cheshire County Council recognised this fact. That public body, though an impartial body, still leaned to the side opposed to him, L, and had a Conservative majerity. Yet they had passed a series of amendments to the Bill that if accepted by the Government would riddle the Bill to such an extent that it would let day- light in at every point. All experts were agreed that what the country desired was an improvement and an extension of secondary education. Yet the Government said virtually, itt You shall spend so much, a sum of 21, on the education and no more." No other country in the world, laid such a charge on the public for educa- tion. By the Bill the people of Runcorn lost control of their technical schisml which had been built partly by gift and partly by loan and to which their best intellects had been devoted. Ao matter how great was the growth of the populatioa the public would have no right to go te that school and say it was their own. The building passed entirely to the County Council. At evening they would have no right to uee it for any pur- pose, even when classes were not lying held. But the measure meted out to the voluntary schools was alto- gether different. The County Council Committee would have control ever the schools only during school hours. The moment the classes left the building it rem tined the property of the present owners. They could have it for parish purpeses and on the Sabbath could use it as they liked. This showed that the one was a privileged school and the other a tied school. The people were despised and the clergy alone were considered. On the voluntary schools the public were to have one third only of the power, which in turn would be seized by the cleric who would be the adviser. There was one adviser not far from toe hall. (Laughter and ap- plause.) The cry of the Tory was that the parent bad a right to educate his child in the religion he wished. That principle he agreed with. But the bill nowhere gave the parent that right. Though the mask was used to cloak its defects the ugly features of clerical ascendency were exposed in it.. In conclusion Sir John said •—" The whole of thleo untry will be ablaze with indignation from one end to the other if the Bill is passed. I warn the Government that if they insist in press ne upon us a Bill which we hate so bitterly from the bottom of our hearts it will be a sad, a sore and a sorry day for the Tory party." (Loud aoplause.) Mr Ellis Griffthe, M.P., in the course of a vigorous speech, condemned the Bill as one which was intended to benefit the Eetablished Geurce. Instead of looking to some pious ancestor for endowment the Church under this Bill was going to the ratepayer and coming down upon the Parish. It was really an attempt to perpetu- ate the power of the priest in the education of this country. (Appiauee.) A resolution containing reasons for rejecting the bi was proposed by Mr Pritchard chairman of the Schoo Board and revised unanimously. It was further resolved that the Chairman sign the petition and give the same to the member for the divisioa kc. Votes of thanks closed the meeting. CATEIOLICS AND THE BILL. MEETING AT RUNCORN.
A well attended meeting was held at St E 'ward's ScheeNon Sunday nigh' t after the evening service, t 3 consider the Education Bill now before Parliament.

The Rev I Chambers addressed the meeting. He said: that to understand the present diffieulties they must go backlto;the year 1870.• Since that time there bad gradual- ly grown a greaterandlgreateoifference between the two kinds of sctaools now in the country. The Board schools were far more favoured than the denominational schools until the last few years, when the aid grant was given to the latter. Thia however, did not make things equal. It was the intention of the present Government to put all the elementary schoole on an equal footing and in the most economical way passible. With the Bill in the main they agreed. It meant justice to both classes of elementary schools. It was net inteaded to destroy Board schoole, which had done, were doing, and would do goad work in the cause of education. It was intended to de away with School Boards and get fram a larger area a wider authority, and, what was hoped to be naturally a better one. Catholics had no quarrel with Board schools, as Such, and as satisfying those parents and ratepayers who desired them. All that Catholies said was that/they dii netjgive them the education they desired, and as parents and ratepayers they could not send their children to them. They could only be satisfied with schaols wherein was taught the Catholic religion alongside the secular education. They (the Catholics) were prepared to provide all new buildings and lend them with those they held at pre- sent for the purpose of education. All they asked was the ripht to appoint Catholic teachers who alone could teach their children their religion, and the control of the religious part of education. For teaching religion there should be no charge, and they would not teach their religion to these children who:might:attend their echools and not desire it. To proselytize was against their very principle. The Rev J Chambers then read and explained the several resolutions which are :—(1) That on no cora- -1 sideration can we give way to the proposal to allow the 1 Local Education or other authorities to nominate more than one-third of the number of managers for a denomi- national school. Such nominee to be on the Board of Management for the purposes of the Education Acts ionic. (2) That the proposal to throw upon the trustees of the school the cost of lighting, warming and cleaning as also that of "ordinary repairs " and "minor improve- ments "—all of which have hitherto been recognised by the Beard of Education as part of " maintenance," chargeable on the grant—must be resisted as destruc- tive. (3) That the Court of Appeal, opera to teachers on dismissal, be to the Board ad Education rather than to the Local Education Authorities, and that if the teacher be dismissed on religious ground the religious tenets or requirements of the denomination to which the echos! belongs be held as sufficient grounds for dis- missal. (4) That no school shall be considered unneces- sary, in consequence of the passing of the Bill, that is at present subject to Government insnection and in the receipt of a Government grant. (5) That the scheme of large areas is preferable to that of smaller ones, of non-county boroughs and urban districts. (6) That the principle of an appeal ts the Board of Education be carefully guarded throughout the Bill. (7) That the optional clause be deleted. -

The resolutions wers pre. p3sed on bloc, seconded, and carried unanimously. The Chairman was instructed to send them to the Matnber for the division and ask his support et these resolutions on the Hill, which contains proposals of suck vital importance to his Catholic constituents.

div.head: Protest Meeting at Earlestown.
div.p: Protest Meeting at Earlestown.

Under the auspices of the Newton-in-Makerfteld Free Church Council, a mestieg to protest against the new Education Bill, was held in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom, Earlestown, on Tuesday evening.—Mr 3 R Profit presided, and 13A was supported by the Revs C Peach, of Manchester, JiMeS Travis, of Chester, E C Bacciekr James AIM% and S D Thomas.—The Chair- man briefly introduced the subject, and the Rev C Peach moved a long and comprehensive resolution to the effect that that meeting protested against the new Education Bill, and they were bound to resist it step by step, as it was a purely sectarian Bill, and must be provocative of much strife. He said if there was one thing more than

another that Free Churchmen were proud of, it was that they never imposed their religious convictions upon the country, never asked any privilege as Free Church:nen, but they should always maintain their right to absolute religious equality with every denomination. Education ought to be free in all its stages, and unsectariam. They heard much about minimise of money being raised by the Church party for day schools but the Nonconformists had raised money for ectiOols, and if they did not use them for day school purposes, they used them for Sunday school purposes and they paid their own way in so using them. In 1870 the School Board system was establietied, and it was distinctly under- stood that it was to be the national system of the country. But now, under this bill the Nonconformists feared they were to be banded over bound hand and foot to the clerical party of the country. The School Board was a popular authority popularly elected, and in place of it, the Government are going to set up another authority which was cot popularly elected, something , entirely unknown to the practice of this country, a committee constituted in a way that no existing author- ity for any purpose whatever has ever been constituted before. A eommittee not publicly elected, will not be under public control. Under the Bill they would have to pay a School Board rate, but they would not get a School Beard. They would have to pay the rate in future, tut would have no voice in the control of the schools. Money which now goes to voluntary schools by voluntary contribution will be liberated and would be available for the building of now schools, or the repairing of fabrics. The Bill was a delusion and a , enare,it does no'hing absolutely for education. A state should be greater than any church, than any class, should hold equal balance between Churchmen and Free Churchmen, between peer and peasant and education should be free to all, and by its means the best mea should come to the top. (Hear, hear.) The Bev James Travis, of Chester, said they had no wish to withheidifrom the Anglian Church any credit due to her for the part she had played in the cause of popu- lar education, and he had great respect for the Anglican Church, as an institution and distinct from the Stad. What they had a right to ask for was a truly National system of education,univereal and free,taught in schools and managed by Boards elected by the people for that purpose alone. The Education Bill was not an educa- tion bill at all, but that was its name. The aim of the bill was to enslave the people and not to improve the education of the people. Who were the opponents of National education ? Not the parents of the children. It was the extreme party in the Anglican Church, and the Priests and Bishops who were fighting them on this matter. Clericalism and Pries:ice-1 had always been the sworn foes of advancement. If Nonconformists were worthy of their ancestr,y and true to their principles they would never rest until they had a system of National education based on civil liberty and religious equality. Revs J Alatt, E C Bocoek and S D Thomas spoke in Support of the resolution which was unanimously carried.
Tae usual votes of than terminated the meeting.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. --- Monthly Meeting.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. --- Monthly Meeting.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural District Council was toll at Bewsey Chambers on Vilednesday afternoon,Nr T Halton presiding. There were also pre- sent :—Dr Murray, Messrs Brooke, Houghton, Knowles, Mather, and Fnehaw, with Dr Sephton (medical officer). Messrs J C Satton (clerk), 5 Sutton (assistant clerk), B S Newcombe (surveyor), U Burnage (assistant sur- veyor), and W Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances).
THE HURAL DISTRICT pauxems ASSOCIATION. THE EDT/CATION BILL.

The CLERK reported that he and the Chairman of the Council (Mr Ball) attended the conference of the Rural District Councils' Association, which included 200 Rural District Conneils. He bad obtained reports of the pro- ceedings at the meeting, and each member of the Coun- cil would receive OSP. The Education Bill was a very important matter which came up for consideration. The meet important question in cuanectien with the Bill was whether the education costs were to fall upon the nation or upon the distriata. The subject was very fully considered and a resolutioa veal pasiel calling upon the government to make the expenses canital charges and not local charges.
DR. SEPETON'S REPORT. THE 'WATER SUPPLY AT HERMITAGE GREEN.

Dr Sephton submiled reports en the health of the District for the past two months. The May report showed that during the month there were 33 births and 19 deaths. Nine of the deaths occurred in Winwick asylum and if these be excluded as not beloneinz tek the die.:riet the death rate would be 11 09 per 1,000. He bad received a cemplaint of very great scarcity of water at Hermitage Green, Croft, and had been requested to bring the matter befere the Ceuncil in order that a better supply might liae obtained. Dr Sephton proceeded to read a letter from Mr Green- ough, who wrote on behalf of most of the inhabitants of Hermitage Green, to seek information as to how an adequate supply of water could be obtained. The epee- tion of the water supply was getting serious. There was only one well and that was three-quarters of a mile away, and it was only by the courtesy of the tenant that the inhabitants of Hermitage Green were allowed to use it. If the well tailed or if the people were stop- ped by the tent nt from using the water the conseqnences would be serioue.

DeS7FHTON laid he believed Hermitage Greel was protected by the Corporat'on Ac% and consocrrentiv the Corporation wouid !nye to supply the district, if the water was being taken in the _pumping operations. _ _
After a short disc7iqaion it W 49 decided 't.hat-tha Cor- psratiou Water Eagineer (Mr Deis) should be written to about the matter.

La his June report, Dr Senhton said there had during Vol month been 15 births anti 24 deaths. Nineteen of the deaths occurred in Win wick Asylum, and if they were excluded, the death rate would be only 5.4. This rate was exceedingly low.. (Bear. hear.)
Tho rep,rt synre adopted. SPECIAL. GRANT FROM THE COUNTY COUNCIL—TRE REBUILDING Or RALTON'S BRIDGE.

ThO SURVEYOR reported the receipt of a letter from the Lancashire County Council to the effect that the re- building nf Halton's Bridge, Sankey, could now be pro- ceeded with, the County Council having made a special grant of £1,364 for the carrying cut of the improve- ment. Toe total amount of the special grants for the year was £2,370, which was £5OO in excess of any previous year's grant. This is equivalent to about sevenpence in the pound.

div.head: Lymm Publican Summoned.
div.p: A Lymm Publican Summoned.

At Lymm Petty Sessions, on Wednesday:, before Mr P Norris, in the chair, Sarah May was charged with permitting drunkenness at the Millstone Hotel, Lymm, on May 23rd. Mr Caldecott prose- cuted on behalf of the police, and Mr Cobbett de- fended.—lt was s tated by the police that in the taproom a man named Percival was asleep, and another named Harrison drunk. The attention of the barman and Mrs May was drawn to the condi- tion of the men, and they both stated that the men the had not been served. It was further added that men bad not been in the house very long. They were not put out because other customers were waiting to be served.—T he case was dismissed on payment of costs.—The two men named were sub- sentiently fined 5s for being drunk.

Sail ord, and Stockport. At the Monmouthshire Under-Sheriff's Court, on Thursday, Florence Kemp was awarded £75 damages for breach of promise and seduction by Walter Stock- I well. The parties were employed by a glass manufac- turing company. AlThe Edinburgh military authorities has just concluded an investigation into a singular affair at 6 Edinburgh Castle, where details of the Royal Elighianders are located. Three shots were one evening fired! from the Castle at the offices near by, one shot piercing a drawer in the office. Six soldiers were arrested, but no one admitted having seen the shots fired. Two men were sentenced to a fortnight's detention for not reporting.

div.head: INVITATION CARD TO THE CORONATION CEREMONY IN WESTMINSTER ABBEY.
div.p: THE INVITATION CARD TO THE CORONATION CEREMONY IN WESTMINSTER ABBEY.

Historians will set down the month of June, 1902, as one of the most notable dates in the annals of the British Empire. Two great events will make it memorable to all time—the pro- clamation of peace in South Africa, which came with its advent, and the Coronation of King Edward VII., which will have taken place ere the expiration of its thirty days. The arrangements for thehistoric festival are now practically tom- plete, and next week the energetic Earl Marshal will be able to announce that everything is ready for his Majesty and the mighty host which will gather to give him greeting when he rides forth To the venerable Abbey and returns a crowned king-, and again when he sets out for the triumphal State parade through the chief city of his magnificent Empire, his Capital of capitals, the centre of his far-reaching dominions, the greatest, wealthiest, and most wonderful city in the world. By the fortunate few only will the artistic card of invitation reproduced here be received, but though the multitude may not be privileged to witness the solemn and stately cere- mony in Westminster Abbey, they will• have opportunities of seeing and saluting their Sovereign, of which they will just as eagerly avail themselves. The route of next Friday's pro- cession is thirteen miles in length, which means, taking both sides of the streets, that the line of spectators will extend for twenty-six miles, and it is safe to say that nowhere from beginning to end will King Edward and his beautiful Queen find a break in the loyal ranks. Their Majesties have seen many enthusiastic demonstrations of loyalty, but that which awaits them next week will eclipse them all.

Old London is hardly recognisable in her festive Coronation garb. Nothing so elaborate in the way of decorations and illuminations has ever been attempted before, and the amount which is being spent on the adornment of the streets by day and by night will constitute a record. The result, from an artistic point of view, shows a gratifying improvement in taste, and not- withstanding the almost incessant rain during the past fortnight, the decorators have succeeded in making the various thoroughfares, especially in the City and West End, look very beautiful. When the finishing touches have been applied, if the weather is favourable the scene will be picturesque beyond description. The list of Foreign Envoys who will be present at the Coronation is a long one, and contains many illustrious names. In addition, our Colonies and dependencies will all be represented, and the con- tingent of distinguished personalities sent to us from abroad will constitute one of the most interesting features in the epoch-making pageant. Most of the Royal guests 16sve already arrived, and
MR. WRITELAW REID.
X NOTABLE ROYAL GUEST AT THE CORONATION :
THE AMERICAN En-or AND BROOK HOUSE, THE LORDLE MANSION RE RAS RENTED FOR THE SEASON.

tiken up their abode in the palatial residences prepared for them, or at the great hotels where luxuriously-furnished suites of apartments were reserved for them months ago. Some of the finest mansions in London have been placed at the disposal of important visitors from across the seas. Mr. Whitelaw Reid, the Special Envoy of the United States, for example, is now making Brook House, Park Lane, Lord Tweedmouth's town house, his temporary home. Brook House is one of the most imposing residences in that street of lordly homes, and it is said that Mr. Whitelaw Reid, who is a very wealthy man, is paying a 'rental of five thousand guineas a month during his occupation of it. By the way, the selection of Mr. Whitelaw Reid as special ambassador of the United States for the Coronation is a particularly happy one. He filled the same office most acceptably at Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, and was United States Minister to France from 1889 to 1892. During his residence in Paris, his entertainments were on a most lavish scale, and he will doubtless do things in princely fashion during the season. Mrs. Reid, formerly Miss Mills, of New York, was a great heiress, and is noted as a delightful hostess. Politically, the appointment of Mr. Reid to the enviable post which he is so well qualified to fill is regarded as a fresh guarantee of the friendship that has been restored between this country and ate great Republic which he represents.

When the momentous event of the crowning of King Edward and Queen Alexandra was first discussed a general idea prevailed that the ceremony would be witnessed by Kings, and perhaps also by one Emperor. The Kaiser William was regarded as a certain visitor, and it was at one time reported that the Czar had promised to eqine if the health of the Czarina was satisfactory. But a glance down the list of envoys from foreign Courts will show that these and other similar surmises, rumours, and reports, all of which filled us with much pleasurable anticipation, have not been ful- filled, nor were they ever likely to be. The etiquette of the occasion does not permit of actual crowned heads participating in the Coronation ceremonies, and there does not appear to be any instance since the reign of Edward I. of an English King or Queen having been crowned in the presence of one of his or her brother rulers. Nevertheless in the Royal progress through London next week, King Edward and Queen Alexandra will be escorted by, an imposing array of Heirs Apparent and Presumptive, so that the public will be permitted to see in the flesh a very large number of the coming generation of Sovereign Princes.

Last Monday the first of the Coronation cele- brations proper took place in the great Review on Laff an's Plain, Aldershot, which was to the Army what the Spithead Review on the 28th will be to the Navy. Though, of course, the fact that none of the troops have yet had time to return from South Africa greatly diminished the numbers which would have been reviewed under ordinary circumstances upon such a great occasion. nevertheless. some

$5,c00 troops mastered under the immediate dm- =Ad of Lieutenant-General Sir Henryllildyard, K.C.8., who isucceecled Sir Redvers Buller as the head of the First Army Corps, and in spite of the wretched weather made a brave show of which the nation has every reason to be proud. The troops consisted of a brigade of cavalry Including the 21st Lancers and Dublin Brigade ..;taff, and commanded by Major-Gen. Hemming, C.B. The King's Yeomanry Brigade was under the oommand of Major-Gen. Right Hon. Lord Chesham K.C.B. There were three batteries of Royal Horse Artillery and fifteen batteries cif Royal Field Artillery, under command of Major-Gen. Sir G. H. Marshall. K.C.8.; the Royal Engineers, commanded by Col. W. Pitt, C.R.E., included a telegraph and bridging battalion. Ist Field Park, 60th Field Com- pany, and oth and 6th balloon sections. The brigade of Royal Marines. ,cominanded by Col-Comman- dant Coffin, was made up of a battalion of Royal Marine Artillery and .one each from Chatham, Gosport, and Plymouth of Light Infantry. The Infantry Divisions were commanded by Major- Generals C. H. IV. Douglas. IL H. Murray, A.D.C., A. H. Paget, C.V.0., H. Hallam Parr, C. 8., C.M.G., ond Sir R. Pole-Carew, K.C.8., C.V.O. The Army iervice Corps and Royal Army Medical Corps were represented. The march past, was immediately ?receded by the presentation of colours to the 2nd Highland Light Infantry, who supplied the guard of honour. The King and Queen had travelled down on Saturday evening with the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Duke
RESIDED.

of Connaught, and other important people, and spent the week-end in Aldershot, occupy- ing the Royal Pavilion for the Brst time. Needless to say, the little Hampshire town fully appreciated the honour which was being done to it, and was en, fae for the whole three days, the entire place being illuminated on Satur- day night for their Majesties' reception, and Our •gaiety being well sustained despite the soaking rain. On Sunday the King was unfortunately laid up with an attack of lumbago, and was unable to attend divine service at All Saints' Church with the Queen and other members of the Royal Family. To everybody's intense regret, his Majesty, al- though much better, was not well enough to carry out the appointed programme on Monday, and the Prince of Wales had to take his place. After the Review the whole of the royal party left for Windsor for Ascot week, the King and Queen. of course, going to the Castle, which has been completely re-furnished and re-decorated for them, whilst the Prince and Princess of Wales took up their quarters at Frogmore House.

A great deal of interest is being taken, both in this country and abroad, in the remarkable case of "Colonel" Arthur Lynch, M.P., who was arrested on a charge of high treason immediately on his arrival in England from the Continent, where he ha been living since his election for Galway City. As the case is sub-judice no com- ments can be offered upon it, but the Solicitor- General's outline of the charge, given before Sir A. de Rutzen at Bow Street La& Saturday' may be quoted, as showing its extraordinary nature. Sir E. Carson said that the charge of high treason alleged against the prisoner was that ha had taken up arms for the late Queen's
AT BOW STREET.

enemies during the progress of the Transvaal War. Mr. Lynch was a British subject, having been born in Australia, and was of Irish descent. He appeared to hate left Australia some ten years ago, and to have been, at all events for some years before the war in South Africa, settled in Paris as a journalist. On the outbreak of the Transvaal War he went to South Africa early in the year 1900, in the capacity of a journalist, though he had undoubtedly been in communication before hia departure with Dr. Leyds, the agent in Europe for the Transvaal Government. Speaking broadly, the case for the prosecution would be that Lynch took up arms for the then Transvaal Government, and raised an armed force known as the 2nd Irish Brigade, of which he appeared to have acted as colonel. In the course of the war he took an active part in the invasion of Natal, and in the operations against General Buller and his army. He also appeared to have been engaged in opera- tions in the Transvaal and elsewhere. Sir E. Carson read a number of letters and documents alleged to have been written by Mr. Lynch, and George Kidney, an ex-member of the Instil Brigade, which the "Colonel" is said to have commanded, gave evidence as to fighting alongside prisoner against the British at Glencoe on March 2nd, 1900. The case was then adjourned, as witnesses have to be brought from South Africa. Mr. Charles Russell is defending Lynch, and the defence is likely to prove not only extremely interesting, but unique in the annaLs of treason trials.
