div.head: COMING CORONATION.
div.p: THE COMING CORONATION.

THERE is Undeniably something exhilarating in the atmosphere of confidence and expectancy which the coming Coronation already brings with it. The Colonial Premiers "GREAT are beginning to arrive, and EXPECTATIONS." with them comes something of the sanguine and buoyant

_ humour of the young populations which they I ' , represent. The Empire seems to be on tiptoe to welcome some greater event than a mere . cere- mony. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has talked a little • vaguely of ,the "transcendent possibilities" of the -, Federation to whicti he would have us "raise our ~ eyes." Tne various Colonial Premiers have res- ponded, each after his fashion. Lord SALISBURY'S grave warning against haste has apparently been overruled ; and while the Loodoo crowd is junket- ing and the KING rides in state, this little group of representative men will dismss the fatefa question in some dim room in Downing-street. It is a magnificent dream, no doubt, this plan for isp. . o making of the E npira a close knit organism of free states. Bat, after all, the strength of the ' x, chain is that of its weakest link. Is the Empire quite ready for the amalgamation ? From any sort of federation India would stand aloof, for we have not even begun to prepare her for the stu- pendous work of self-government. Ten years hence, perhaps, South Africa may be a Common- wealth as free and united as Canada or Australia; but that day is not yet. There is neither moral worth nor security in a federation which should not rest on consent. And what consent could we

_ expect from the two new colonies which have not yet acquired from the conqueror the right to say "aye" ,or "nay"? vSo far lar3 we from the goal that the cry is even now for the destruction of the Constitution under which Cape Colony has lived for a generation. So little confidence have our Imperialists in their work that they ask us to destroy the Cape Parliament, because they cannot be sure that a majority of English blood can be reckoned on its benches. It is a retrograde and even a perfidious step, since in November, 1899, Sir ALFRED lklnxnu,:replying to a rumour that some sach plot was:in the air, gave a definite promise that the Government would always respect the Constitution. It is a question on which the whole future trust of the Boar race in our honour mast depend, and no federation, however complete, would compensate us for the loss of that confidence. But even these are not our only pre-occupations. Ireland casts her gaunt shadow of poverty and discontent over these Coronation festivities— tie lovely anl tile lonely Bride Whom we have wedded, bM have never won. While Colonial Premiers are riding in the Corona- tion procession, Mr. REDMOND and Mr. DILLON, with a score of,their lieutenants, will be standing in the dock under the ;:Coercion Act, without a Jury, to be tried by removable magistrates for championing the cause of the miserable peasantry of the Weat_the poorest, the most neglected, the' most hopeless peasantry out of Russia. And crowning irony of all, while we are preparing to grant the Boers self government -government because without it they never will be loyal, to the Irish we refuse it. Here are problems enough to busy the Imperialist. It is folly to federate before Nye have enfranchised. That would be the hasty work of a jeweller who should strine, uncut diamonds.

Bur it is the least objection to this scheme of Imperial Federation that it seems premature. The means by which it is to be brought about would be fatal to our destiny. " The THE PRICE. Empire," Mr CHAMBERLAIN once told us, " is commerce," and accordingly its federation is to be '3ased on commercial ties. Wa are to make it worth while for the Colonies to federate with us by abandon- ing Free Trade, admitting their products duty-free -while we levy a tarift upon those of „other coun- tries, in return for which they are to give our goods a preference in their custom houses. Now, this plan would be feasible on two conditions : (1) If the Colonies among them were able to supply us with all the food we require and all the raw material which our commerce requires ; (2) if the slight gain which a preference would bring us in their markets would compensate us for the loss of our;foreign trade, Neither of these conditions can be satisfied. We get much of our wheat from Canada and muck: of our timber, a great deal of meat from New Zealand, and most,

hat by no means all, of our wool from Australia ; while the Cotton that comes from India, Egypt, Cyprus, .tc., is insignificant. Our exports to our Colonies, though considerable, are in value barely a third of all we send abroad. What then would be the result of a preferential tariff ? Simply to raise the pricer' of our foodstuffs. We can diminish the profits of America, but we cannot dispense with her supplies. We can enhance the profits of the Colonies, but we cannot buy from them all we require. If food is dear, however, either wages will rise or the working man will be poorer. And if wages rise it will be impossible to compete w:th the foreigner in neutral markets. Further,if if we were so infatuated as to tax wool and cotton, we should at one blow destroy the trade of York- shire and Lancashire. To tax timber, again,would aggravate the housing question, burden ship- building, and harass coal-mining, in which wooden props are necessary. And what should we gain ? The Jingoes tell us that in time of war we ought not to rely on foreigners for our food supplies. Well, we buy wheat from America, from Russia, and from Hungary. Are we ever to go to war ' with all these Powers at once ? So long as vc.e command the sea we can always import wheat. And if we lost our supremacy at sea it would be as difficult to fetch corn from Canada as from the States. It is the maddest scheme that ever dis- tracted the brain of a politician. Even to toy with it is national suicide.

THE great demonstration in London against- the Education Bill, at which Lord ROSEBERY, who has never been suspected of a Nonconformist con- science, stood on the same AUTUMN' platform as Mr LLOYD- LEAVES. GEORGE, has clearly caused certain of the more intelligent Ministerialists to reflect. A day or two later Mr BALFour., treated a great deputation from the Free Churches to the usual exibibition of con- tempt, but somehow he failed to raise the usual chorus of applause from the usual Conservative organs. Here are the outspoken comments of the "Morning Post," which speaks for fashionable Toryism: How, then, did Mr. Balfour meet them? Ec treated them to a lecture on their narrow-minded- ness in not toeing delizhted with his bill. He wos not prepared with any suggestion that he could inset them half-way; he did not find it possible to pat himself for a moment at their point of view. Foe bill was the only possible bill; triers was no alternative. . . . These tacdcs appear to us to be misplaced. It was quite right when dealing with the Boers lately in arms for the Government t dic- tate the terms, and to admit of no modification of them. But tttet is hardly a precedent for dealing with those who represent, if not half, at any rate a considerable portion of our own people. No wonder the impression gains ground that an Autumn Session will be necessar: to carry this Bill. In autumn it may seem natural to shed some leaves from this precious document.

Not even the approaching Coronation and the holidays it will bring have been so much talked about during the week as the weather everywhere experienced. To-day is the longest day of the year "by the calendar" as one of Shakespeare's characters puts it, "and from Jane 21st we are to expect a good deal of rain, preceded by numerous thunderstorms, and the weather will be zompara- tively cool," says Professor Falb, who has gener- ally something startling or uncanny to tell us,and is, happily for us, often deceived. All the things promised "from the 21st," to-day, we have been expericncing the past six weeks! But that he had already told us May would be "cold and wet," one would nave concluded that he had skipped six weeks of the almanac to:to-day. Turning to a more comforting assurance of the Meteorological Office, one finds that, according to the weather forecast, there is a prospect of" a gradual improvement with an increase of temperature," and, therefore one is not disposed to call "a plague on both your houses" yet; though the house of Falb has often seemed to deserve it. As there really seemed no chance lately of our having any summer at all, even the belated departure of winter will be wbl- come. But it is a fearful and wonderful thing to learn that there is still a deficiency of an inch and a-half in the average rainfall for the year. It would not be proper for a mere layman to ex- press scepticism, but it may be safe to say with gentle firmness, that the rain gauge seems in a fair way to earning the unenviable reputation of the gas meter, or sharing the fate of "the dog with a bad name."

The surrender of the Boer commandos proceeds tranquilly and without incident. But it serves aptly enough to prove the absolute ignorance in which this war has been conducted. A year ago 31iBrodrick told us that there were only 10,000 Boers in the field. According to Lord Kitchener's weekly" bags," we have since accounted for over 8,000 of this number killed or captured. There ought, therefore, to be less than 2,000 left. In point of fact, over 17,000 have surrendered, and the process is not yet complete. The ridiculous optimism in which the war began persisted to the end. •

It is useless for Sir Michael Hicks-Beach to pre- tend that the tax on flour does not disturb ourl fiscal system, or to plead in its vindication that honesty compels it. The concession as to maize, dropping at a stroke £300,000, makes the revenue still more ridiculous in proportion to the Ex- chequer gain it brings and it was pointed out by Mr Morley that if the Chancellor's motive were simply to broaden the basis of taxation he has al- ready paid sufficient attention to articles weighing on trade and labour. This Government had put six and a-half millions on sugar, two millions on tea, and two millions on the coal tax, before introduc- ing the corn tax which is to yield two and a-half millions. The additional burden of ten and a-half millions should have been deemed suffici3nt to remind the people of their responsibilities, and to check khaki fever. Mt Morley, who holds strong views about the spirit of militarism, thinks that the Chancellor's per- formance was adequate without touching the loaf. As a measure of emergency something might be said for this impost, but as a lasting burden it is not only bad in policyi but vexatious in opera- tion. If the consumer had to pay only what falls to the Exchequer, he would have less cause for in- dignation, but he has to pay not only on the corn from which the Chancellor raised the revenue, but on corn which yields nothing extra in the way of revenue. He has, in fact, to give a special bene- fit to one particular trader as well, who thus profits at the expense of the community. The manufacturers of Lancashire realise what that means. Labour is one of their materials in the Process of manufacture, and what pinches the worker has a harmful effect on them. Thus their profits and their ability to compete with foreign manufacturers must be still further curtailed. This is not the way to maintain Great Britain's prosperity as the workshop of the world.

" Mafficking and rowclyismaanrsee7r to a letteroknownin Warrington," says the 11,1airaiy ,sTw, h Mayor in w Iron' the editor of the , en- gaged in preparing an article to teach the people is ° W of Britain how to revel. As arringtn is a typical Lancashire town withworking-class a population, Mr Gardiner, who has only just left Blackburn for London, will be inclined to reproach himself for having imagined for a moment that there could be either " Mafficking " or rowdyism in Warrington, and to him the Mayor's letter must come as a mild reproof. Lancashire crowds are notoriously quiet, orderly, and undemonstrative, and it seems a pity that the necessity should have arisen to remind Mr Gardiner of the fact. A moment's reflection must have convinced him of the needlessness of applying here for samples of

national rejoicings "boisterous or even un- mannerly." We require no instruction in the art of " how to revel." " Glad tidings of great joy" we receive with that philosophic calm typical of Lancastrians, and as for revelling "—why, the mere congratulatory shako of the hand one with another amply suffices. We can imagine the pained surprise of His Worship at the bold suggestions contained in the letter of this inquisitive editor, and we rejoice that he was able to so completely dispel the notion that there ever was, is now, or is ever likely to be the faintest approach to rowdyisim in Warrington. " Maffick ! "indeed, Tut ! Tut !

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY JUNE 20, 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY JUNE 20, 1902
MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

Provincial towns were satisfactorily represented at the Review of the Boys' Brigades on Saturday, the somewhat unpromising weather notwithstand- ing. It must have been a real treat to the boys to take part in an inspection in the quadrangle of the Horse Gnards by the Prince of Wales. It consti- tuted the apotheosis indeed, for the time being, of a movement that was commenced not many years since, but one that has enchained the popular fancy in a marvellous degree. The whole of the proceed- ings were highly successful,the simple evolutionary movements being executed with a precision that evoked the approval of a vast concourse of specta- tors. It was made very clear that the movement has excited the interest of both old and young, a truth to which the large company of military officers on the ground sufficiently testified. It should be duly noted in the provinces, also, that the Royal review ! will give a still further impetus to the organisation, which mustfnecessarily prove greatly advantageous to the Volunteers, since it will be a natural step from the ranks of the Boys' Brigades to those of the Volunteers when the lads have attained the age that would justify such transference. The Prince did not deliver any address to the lads who passed under his notiee on Saturday, but it was under- stood that his Royal Highness was much gratified by their smartness and geveral appearance. Some thousands of them had travelled all the way from fcotlaud to be present at an assembly that will in future days rank as historic in the annals of the movement. It may be added that the Boys' Brigade movement, which had to en- counter no little disparagement in its earlier stages, is now an assured success. As an American would put it, " it has come to stay," and it should prove a valuable recruiting ground both for the volunteers and the regulars, as well as confer marked advan- tages on those who participate in the periodical drills. It will also tend in the direction of warding off suggestions and proposals in certain quarters regarding conscription,

For a fortnight or more mysterious hints have been current that the Provincial Tour of the Colon- ial Premiers would be wholly abandoned. Most newspaper readers had naturally come to the con- clusion that the pre-Coronation tour had been most unsatisfactorily arranged. It was found on ex- amination that frequently the engagements made by the Prerniers,and by others on their behalf,over- lapped ; while some of the fixtures on the programme had been arranged for dates long before those on which the majority of the Premiers were timed to arrive in this country. Still there was an impression that, despite the pre-Coronation mis- management, the engagements made for dates after the Coronation week would be kept. But it has since transpired that the scheme of provincial visits has b&en abandoned in its entirety ! It is only too evident that there has been a perplexing game of cross-purposes in operation, the result of which will be teat the Colonial Premiers, as a body, will have no opportunity of meeting their friends in the provinces, or of seeing to what extent the extra- metropolitan industries contribute to the prosperity and stability of the Empire. To say that this is extremely disappointing is to put the matter much too mildly. It is distinctly and emphatically unfair to the pro- vinces, from which Llndon draws much of its wealth and many of its met brilliant and capable men in all the higher ranks and, avocations. One had been expecting to hear by this time that a joint appeal direct to the Colonial Premiers had been formulated and submitted, with a view to per- suade them to consent to the re-zasting of their programme. Meanwhile the representatives of the Australian Commonwealth, New 7. >aland and other Colonies have arrived, while others are on the point of arrival, and it is gratifying to learn that some of these have already agreed to visit certain of the cites and towns of the provinces to which they have been formally and promptly invited.

The statement that Generals Louis Botha, De Wet,and Delarey are coming to Europe next month will raise the hope that the " übiquitous " one will accompany Botha when the latter comos7to Eng- land, as he proposes to do after visiting Holland. If the two should extend their visit to the pro- vinces, no one will think less of Da Wet for the evident pain and regret with which he has accepted the new Government. He does accept it, however. and he is a man of his word. But, how the sur- renders continue to confound all previous calcula- tions ! By this time they will probably number twenty thousand ; so that, what becomes of Mr Brodrick's estimate of last December? Better be had said sometimes that be " didn't know." For it has also to be pointed out that since there are these surrenders, and there are twenty-five thousand prisoners, to say nothing of National Scouts, and killed and wounded, and foreigners who have re• turned to Europe, the Boer forces at one time must have vastly exceeded the " handful of farmers " of which the lovers of other countries rather than their own have been so given to speaking.

Postal arrangement s.for the provinces on the. two Coronation holidays will have to be seen to at once by many of us. On Thursday, the 26th, the post offices will be open to the public the same hours as on Sundays; and at offices, not being town sub. offices, which de not ordinarily open on Sundays, , the attendance will be from eight till ten o'clock in the usornihg, and between these hours telegraphic messages may be despatched and received at offices which transact that kind of bibiness. Town sub- offices will be closed, and there will be only one de- livery and collection of letters on the day specified. Postal business on Friday, the 27th, will be regulat- ed precisely as on a Bank Holiday. It is plain, of course, that the whole business of the country , cannot be suspended, and the arrangements made seem designed to reduce the number of persons on duty to a minimum. The one delivery and col- lection in the towns will presumably he in the morning, and all persons employed at rural offices will have the day to themselves after ten o'clock. But it is upon the telegraphic staffe in centres of populations served by daily newspapers that the chi 4 burdens will fall. The telegraphic service throughout the provinces will be taxed to its utmost limit. The occasion will be unprecedented in the history of telegraphy,for no Coronation of a British Sovereign has taken ',place since the telegraphic system was established. Probably the Government will find some means of compensating those who will not only have to work on the two great holi- days, but will have previously to brace themselves for so special and onerous a task.

Mr. Chaplin, erstwhile a Tory of the Tories, and Fair Trader to boot, but a kind of political nondes- cript since Lord Salisbury relieved him of office, in addressing Mr. Balfour the other day, expressed the characteristic idea that "inasmuch as the better country people were educated the more Were they disposed to leave the land, whereas agricultur- ists wanted to keep people on the land." It is difficult to believe that a dull and ignorant farm assistant even is as valuable as one who, having his capacities developed by a good elementary educa- tion, has the ability to profit by the technical instruction in agriculture which ought to be general in agricultural districts. The agricultural labourer who has to manage motor wagons, and by-and-bye motor ploughs, together with other kinds of labour— saving machinery, will be worth much more than the ignorant kind of former days, and it will pay his employer to recognise this. It is only fair to say that Mr Balfour did not afford Mr Chaplin much encouragement. and the matter is mentioned here by way of directing the attention of provincial educationists to the party to whom the educational interests of the country are at present entrusted.

The question of making application for extension of hours on Coronation Day was discusEed, and it was unanimously decided that no application for Extension of hours be made, and that all members be nofnied to that effect. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
[Br A. CORRESPONDENT].

'..iotor cycles are all very well in their vziy, and may perhaps be an easy and rapid method of tran- sit, but when a novice tries to manage one, well, he may think a little differently about the pleasures of motoring. The other day an inhabitant went for a spin on one, and all went well for a time, at least whilst he alowed the machine to have its own way, but as soon as he attempted to take it under control, the result was disastrous to both. He never antici- pated, when he started off with a complacent smile on his face that the cycle would display any temper. But it did ; not only did i refuse to go the way he wished it to go. but it trieu to climb a wall, not easily and gently, but with a rush, as if it was determined to get to tbe top. The motorist was not given,to climbing walls in that fashion,so he gracefully dism4uated, fortunately without serious injury. Not so the bike; it got somewhat the worst of toe affray in its encounter with the wall, with the result that:it lrad to be whealed home in a handcart. Rather an undignified return.

The C)roantion festivities at Earlestovrn and Newton will be .on a first class scale, and tha pro- cession which is being organised will not be a whit behind any others of the kind in point of dis- play. They don't do things by the halves in this neighbourhood and the invitation of the Committee te the people to observe the occasion with enthusiasm will certainly be observed to the full. A flue day is earnestly hoped for.

COOKERY LECTURES AT ELRLEST3NVN.

Under the auspices of the Newtou—in-Makerfield Council, au exaibit ion of gas stoves was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown on Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday this week. The firms exhibit- ing were Messrs Wright and Ca., Mews Fletcher , Russell:and Co., and Mess:s Richmonds. The Dis- trict Council have decided to supply any of the three makes of stoves to residents on the hire pur- chase system and to fix them free of charge, the purchase money to extend over a period of five years. To display the merits of the variots stoves, cookery lecturts were given in the afternoon and evening of each day, and demonstrations to show how easy it is to do all classes of csokiog on a gas range. The ex- hibition was opened by Mr W Thompson, chairman of the Gas Committee, who briefly explained to those present the reasons for the holding of it. Miss Li U Tuxford afterwards proceeded with her lecture and demonstrations of cookery, and some valuable information to housewives was given. The exhibi- tion was fairly successful and no doubt there will be a good after result.

div.head: A.' SUCCESSFUL DEFENCFI.
div.p: A.' SUCCESSFUL DEFENCFI.

At the Warrington County Patty Sessions on Wednesday, Henry Billings, Porter-streearring- ton, was charged with stealing three pairs of ladies' boots and two odd ladies' boots from the shop o Birkhead Bros., 7, Earle-street, Earlestowni on the ,114th June. —Jane Bracken, a servant in the employ of the prosecutors, spoke to seeing the prisoner in i a passage adjoining the shop on the date in ques- tion.—Frank Birkhead said that at about ten o'clock in the evening he went outside his shop to take in a " stick of 'boots." He heard someone moving about in the entry at the side,and on going there found the prisoner with one of the boots lying close to his feet. One of witness's tickets was on the boots. When asked what he was doing there he said he was waiting for a friend who had gone tor a drink. On entraining the stick witness found several boots were mis-ing. They I;',were afterwards found concealed some distance away.— PC Hughes said that when he took prisoner into custody he said "I am done again on another soft job." Witness found six of the boots in question about forty yards away from the shop. On being charged prisoner said he had not touched a boot. Prisoner now said he waswalking along Earle-street and saw some people whom he knew coming along. As he did not wish to speak to them he stepped into the entry, and had been there only two or three minutes when Mr Birkhead came out. He knew nothing about the boots.—The Bench decided to give prisoner the benefit of the doubt and dis- missed the case.

div.head: Local Wesleyan Methodism.
div.p: Local Wesleyan Methodism.

Toe qoarterly meeting of the Warrington Wesleyan Methodist Circuit was hc/d in the Moore WE s:eyan Church on Monday. There was a very large gathering of members at a tea which was kindly provided by the Moore friends. The tables were beautifully decorated with choice plants and flowers. provided by Mr and Mrs Birch, The schoolroom was adorned in a most tasteful Manner with flags and flowers by the ladies. A corn- prebensive vote oi thanks was moved on the propos'tioa of the circuit stewards, Messrs J W Hayward and G Weaver, and heartily carried. Miss B Rotten, Messrs Birch and Roylance replied.— The Rt.v T Bishop presided over the meeting held in the church situ. tea. The Secrete:3r, Mr W Sileock,read the minutes, which were confirmed. Mrs;ages of sym- ' pathy were, sent to Mr R Garnett and Mr Lawton, who were absent through il nese. A long discussion took Islam as to the advisability of selling Hatton Chapel. in which Messrs Corbett, Meldrum, Littler, G Weaver, E Richardson and Norman took part. It was eventually decided to leave the matter in the hands of the trustees. The senior circuit steward. Mr J W Hayward, presented the financial statement, which showed • balance in hand of £l2. The Chairman presented tbe membership re- turns. These showed a total of 893, an increase of three. The Secretary read letters from the Rev W Carom (Birmingham), an Rev E Wilkin Rees (Manchester). accept- ing the invitations sent them to become the successors of the Revs T Bithap and C H Hocken. These two gentlemen were very heartily thanked for their three years, services in the circuit, Many members spoke of their efficient work and pastoral care, nor were the ser- vices of Mrs Bishop and Mrs Beckon, which have been very great, forgott.m. The two reverend gsntlemen very feelingly replied. The Chairman renorted that Martins- croft Chapel bad been re-opened after extensive altera- tions, which had cost about £350, and only £4O remained to be raised. Permission was given for the erection of a caretaker's house at Padgate at a cost of £250. Noptogress has been made with the Stockton Heath scheme. It was decided to make collections in all the chapels in the circoit for the Local Preachers' Mutual Ai. . Association. A committee was appointed to consider tile case of Bostock-street mission. The next quart srly meeting is to be held at Lymm.

RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.

In c3mmon with other towns Ruucurn is " Coronation mad." The decorations of the trades- men's shops and the• animas' dwelling houses promise to beggar destription. They are to be on a much more lavish scale than ever previously attempted. rhe rhalry between the Anglicans and the Nonconformists stii: continues to be a fruitful theme for idlers to dilate upon. liappily the rivalry is now clothing itself in a more agreeable guise. Each of the Sunday schools is striving night and morn in honourable competition to outclass the other numerically and spectaculary. There will be some rare sights on Coronation Day.

The Runcorn Shorthand Writers Association whose birth was heralded with such a flourish of trumpets is n3w no more. This sudden demise is to be deplored. The association's unilmely end has, howeyer, been hastened by the apathy of the indivilual member and not through the supineness of the official. Messrs Bridges and Tdmkins, secretary and ill-librarian respec- tively, have both performed their duties admirably. and no blame devolves upon them. The immedi- ate effect of the winding up of the Association is to close another outlet—and there are not too many outlets in Runcorn—by which the intellectual energy of the youth of Runcorn at one time found vent. Meanwhile there is evidence that society will be more blessed in its end than its beginning. Its library has been conveyed to the Runcorn Library, and as th-re is a good demand for shorthand litera- ture, the Society, though defunct through its works, will be more influential ia its death than in its life.

The I helwall nuisance still attractssattention al- though the Rural Council are tired of the subject. Mr Naylor wrote a mug letter in reply to the state ments made by Inspector Farrington that the nuisance emanated from Mr Naylor's own house, but the Council decided not to read it. From the discussion which ensued it appears that Mr Naylor has written to each member of the Council respecting his complaint, even going so far in the case of the inspector as to partly threaten him with legal proceedings in consequesc of his assertions at the last meeting. The nuis- ance inspector in defence stated that he was then wrongly reported by the pres. This is hardly correct. The press in common with the councillors received the impression from Mr 14 arrington that the sewage smell emanated from Mr Naylor's sett- ling tank which was choked up in consequence of an overflow from tenements further up the road. It was distinctly stated 'by someone that had Mr Naylor been at home the tank would not have got choked up. The Council were discussing the origin of a smell which had long existed; not, as Mr Farrington would assert, the contingency of some smell which might be traced to the settling tank. No amount of' ifs " to qualify the rsported phrase can dispose , of the difficulty.

Good Templary. The No 1 Convention of South-West Landashire met for their monthly session at the Hope of Sutton Lodge, St Helens Junctiou, on Saturday last. The Convention was opened at 330 by Bro Lindon. A large representative gathering was assembled, re- pres.entatires from Wigan. Leigh, St Helens, War- rington, Widnes,Earlestown,llope ofut',on,St:Helens Pioneer.Runcorn and others puttiug in an appear- ance. A spirited session was held and good work reported. After tea, Bro Clartre,of Earlestown,read a paper giving a history of the No 1 Convention, which proved interesting and encouraging,and was accorded a vote of tank s for his paper.:During the 'evening an open air, and afterwards an indoor, .1 public meeting were held, when Bro Lea of Liver- pool and Bro Parr of Leigh gave addresses ann a capital programme was rendered, resulting in several pledges being taken.

Warrington Workingmen's Angling Association. The Warrington Workinvnun's Anglin; Associa- tion opened the season with a match last week end the members and friends journeying in 'buses to Barrow Lock, where the match was held. There was not:much:sport, the fish being whqt anglers generally term "off." The first prize was won by by Mr W Whitfield,2ud Mr T Lea, 3rd Mr C Haslam. Fifty-two took part in the match but only 17 suc- ceeded in catching fish. The prizes was given out on Monday night and after the business was over the membsrs had a very enjoyable evening. It is hoped to have another match shortly, through the generosity of the President, Mr II Mather, who has off.red the Association £5 towards expenses and has promised to give .£5 a year towards prizes. div.head: DEATH OF MR. PERCY FAIR.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. PERCY FAIR.
A Pathetic End.

News reached Warrington on Thursday last week of the painfully sudden death on board ship at Southampton,of Slr.Percy William Fair who up to about seven years ago resided in Lovely-lane. The circumstances attending his death are singu- larly pathetic. Just as the steamship Paul from New York was nearing port at Southampton he was seen to drop down dead on deck. He had undertaken the voyage in the hope of recruiting his health which had broken down under the rigours of life in Klondyke, where he owned a claim. The cause of death was investi- gated by a Coroner's jury at Suuthampton yester- day and a verdict of" Death through failure of the heart's action was returned." It is thought that the momentary excitement of seeing the home land once more, combined with his weak condition,were responsible for his sudden collapse. When in Warrington Mr Fair was a well-known cyclist and won many laurels on the racing path. He was a prominent member of the Cycling Club, and the news of his death will occasion deep regret to his former club mates. He was also an adept at boxing, and frequently took part in displays at the Gymnasium. He was 36 years of age, and for many years was employed in the office at Whitecross Works. His parents and members of the family reside at Padgate and Warrington. The body will be brought to Warrington to-day, and the funeral will take place to-morrow unday) afternoon in St Paul's Churchyard.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral of the late Mr Percy William Fair (eldest son of Mr John Fair, of Padget.), whose painfully sudden death on board ship at South- ampton was reported in our last issue, took place at St Paul's Caurch on Sunday 'afternoon. The cortege was met ratjthe churchyard gate in Paul-street by the Vicar (the Rev W Bracecamp) and some of the members of the choir. The body of the church was quite full during the service, and even the galleries were occupied, the congregation being larger than has been seen at any funeral service held in this church for a considerable number of years. The deceased at one time was a noted athlete, and the local clubs were well represented at the funeral. The hymn sung was "A few more years shall tell," and before the service in church was concluded the Vicar addressed the congregation. In the course of his remarks he said that Brother Fair had been taken away in the prime of life,and if his sad death induced any of those present to lead a different life it would have been blessed of God No doubt the mourners thought it was very bard Mr Fair should be removed when he was looking forward to reach- ing home and shaking his relatives and friends by the hands, and they might be inclined to say "It is too bad," but he wished to tell them for their com- fort that whatever God had done was for the best though they might not see it. The proceedings at the graveside were of an especially solemn char- acter. The coffin was almost hidden from view by beautiful floral tributes of respect, while a carriage in the funeral procession was filled with othe•a The chief mourners were Mr and Mrs John Fair,Mr J H Fair, Mr Stanley Fair, Mr and Mrs Povey (brother-in-law and sister), Mr and Mrs Ballard, Miss M Fair, Miss Ethel Fair, Miss Beatrice Fair, and Mr S Ballard. Others present were Mr Edwin Green, Councillor John Evans, Mr H H Evans, Mr Arthur Allen, Mr J Buxton, Mr J Craik, Mr C Bollingworth, Mr W llRellian, Mr John Bellian, Mr Percy Bradburn, Mr H Mackay, Mr E Chambers and Mr T Partridge. Wreaths were sent by "1 ether and Ellen," " Lizzie and Julian," "John and Emily," "Stanley and Louie," "Maud, Ethel, Gerty, and Beatrice," Lilly, Gerty and Minnie Green, Councillor J. div.head: NOTES ON (JAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON (JAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Warrington sustained their first reverse of the season on Saturday, St Helens being the team to check their triumphant career. The innings of the Warringtonians was productive of only 85 runs, whilst at seven o'clock the St Helens eleven had run up the substantial aggre- gate of 127 for the loss of nine wickets. The result was in a great measure due to the splendid batting of Foreman and Turner, the first-named player being res- ponsible for 51, and Turner for 49. Woodley gave the Warrington batsmen considerable trouble, and captured 5 wickets for 31 runs. The St Helens eleven are doing exceptionally well this season, a strong team from Old Trafford falling victims to their prowess last week.

Had it not been for the highly creditable batting of J Gibbon, the Warringtonians would have made a very poor show indeed. This player rattled up a total of 44 by stylish cricket, his strokes including one six, five fours, and two threes. P. B. Hawtin with 10 was the only other batsman to attain double figures, so it will be seen that the general batting display was below the average.XJ. W. Bibby, the Warrington captain, had the misfortune to be bowled for one, and Lynes, the professional, made only five.

The feature of the St Helens inn rigs was the brilliant play by Turner and Foreman. Changes of bowlers were tried for a considerable time without avail, but event- ually Turner failed to negotiate a delivery from Connor, and was bowled after compiling 49. Foreman continu- ed to play with great vigour, but Briggs got him out with a simple ball, when he had run up 51.
The Warrington bowling analysis reveals no extra- ordinary achievements. Lynes did not come np to his usual form, taking only one wicket at a cost of 29. Bibby took one wicket for 31.

How have the mighty 1 alien Cheshire Lines Engineers had at one time a high reputation in the district, and their encounter with Warrington Wesleyans on Saturday furnished a great surprise. The Engineers were dismissed for the absurdly small total of 4. Five wickets fell without a run being scored and nine wickets were down for two runs. The last wicket added another two. Doody and Hewitt were responsible for the downfall of the Engineers, the former taking five wickets for two runs and the latter four for two. The catch with which Gorst dismissed Howard was an exceptionally brilliant one and elicited a roundof applause.

Foot Racing. There were numerous local successes at the athletic festivals held in the district on Saturday. At Earles- town, E. Harris, the Warrington footballer, carried off the first prizes in the 100 and 220 yards handicap, and H D Gibson won a second prize in the 440 yards local. Four prizes were won by members of the Sankey Harriers. L. Green was an easy winner of the first prize in the 440 yards handicap at Winnington Park, and he also won the third prize in the 100 yards event. At the sports held in connection with the St. Helens Recreation C.C., T. Devlin and R. Gibson (Sankey Harriers),were awarded the second and third prizes res- pectively in the one mile race.

div.head: "Daly News" and the Mayor
div.p: The "Daly News" and the Mayor
Testimonial for Warrington.
Tho followirs! interestinff correspondence has passed between the Mayor and the Editor of the "Daily News " The " Daily News " Office. London, June 1902.

Dear Sir,— We have noted with some regret the tendency,especi- ally in our large cities, for national rejoicings to become unduly boisterous, and even unmannerly ; and we find that responsible citizens of all parties deprecate certain incidents, known popularly as " Maffieking," and re- peated during the peace celebrations, In view of the Coronation, we are enquiring in many quarters what is being done and what can be done to guide the people in their legitimate expression of joy. We propose to collate tho resu!t; under the title " How Britain Should Revel," and we invite your suggestions, as welt as an) infor- mation you may be able to supply, especially in refer- ence to drawing the crowds away from the public bowies and streets, into the parks, through the agenc'l of illumination and military bands. Yours faithfully. A. G. GARDINER, Editor. The Mayor of Warrington.
Town Hall, Warrington. June 11th, 1902.

To the Editor of the Daily New?. Dear Sir,— In reply to your communication lam happy to say " MafEckinc• and Rowdyism " are unknown in War- rington. On the eoo4sion of the Declaration of Peace on Monday the 2nd instant lam told there were 30,000 people assemb'ed in front of the Town Hall and in the streets adjtcent at 9 p.m. Not a single untoward incident occurred to my knowledge. The announcement from the Town Hall steps was greeted with cheers from the crowd who then joined heartily in the National Anthem and after a snort display of fireworks the immense concourse quietly dispersed and the record at the Police Court the next mottling was nil. Yours faithfully, J CHARLTON PARR, Mayor.

WARRINGTON. The Widening of Kendrick-street. The improvement which is being effected by the widening of Kendrick-street proceeds very slowly. The provision of new gates at the Froghall-lane end of Crosfield-street, the widening of Kendriek- street a?, far as the old entrance into the park from that street, and the building of a new stone wall, surmounted with iron palisades,bas been completed after much delay. It has now been decided to remove a further portion of the brick wall and sub- stitute iron palisades. Sir H Fairclough has secured the contract and will proceed immediately with the work. During the past week two large tress behind the park potting shed have been felled ia order to facilitate the work,

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
TERRE MONTHS' IMPRISONMENT FOR A NEGLECTFUL MOTHER.

At the Warrington County petty Sessions on Wednesday. Mary Hankinson, Hollins Hreen, was charged with neglect- ing her four children in a manner likely to Cause them unnecessary offering and injury to health.--Mr Brown• prosecuted on behalf of the NSPC p, and said the prisoner was the wife of a very respectable .man living at Hollins- green, who earned El per week as a labourer. Two sons were working and brought in 10s per week each, utaking a total of Despite that she pawned everything for drink. Inspector Hackett had from time to time wanted her and she only laughed at him. On Mon lay Mr Auld and, school attendance officer, visited the house and the children were in such a deplorable condition that he at once reported the matter to Inspector Hackett, The Inspector visited the house in company with P C Clarke. The woman appeared to have had soma drink and was in a very dirty state. The child Margaret, who was thirteen years of age, Wee very poorly nourished and badly c'othed. The was filthy dirty and " alive with lice." Her body Was copper coloured and her bead was verminous. The bay Arthur was very well nourished and fairly well clad, but the clothing was dirty. His body was fairly clean bat had lice upon it. The boy James was at school, aid the se.hoolmaster said he had had to send the children home time after time as they were not fit to mix with the other children. James was in a filthy and vermiaous condition, and the other ehild Albert, • was also verminous The house was fairly well furnished, and the husband said he " could not put up with the state of affairs any longer." He would undertake to look after the children. Evidence was given, and prisoner Was sent to g•ol for three months.

_ BITING A FOLIC EMIN.— %LIU Lynch. a young !woman living in Bank-street, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Union-street, at ten minutes past one on Sunday morning, and also with having assaulted P C. Clarke in Buttermarket-street,at a quarter past one.—The Constable said the prisoner came to him and P.C. Corbett in Bank- street, and asked for lodgings. They directed her te a lodging-house, when she began to use very filthy language, and refused to go away. Thee took her into custody and she West quietly as far as Academy-street. he there hit witness in the mouth, and threw herself down. She after- wards bit his hand, and was most violent all the way to the Police Station.—P C Corbett and Sergeant Smith gave corroborative evidence, and prisoner was sent to gaol for a month.

_ STItiIIET BETTING AT RUNCORN.—BAD CASE.—Henry Horton was charged at the instance of Superintendent Hnnion with frequenting a certain place for the par oose of betting on the 27th May and other dates.—Mr H F Neale. of Liverpool, defendet—Seargeant Gregory deposed that at 11 45 am on the 31st May defendant was standing in Station-road near the railway station. At 125 witness saw three men go to the defendant and hand him some paper; at 12.15 afmther man came up and handed defendant a paper ; at 12 25 two men did the same; at 12.30 one man did likewise; at 1.5 one man - at 1.23 two men ; at 1.26 one man; at 1.401w0 men. Defendant then left and went down Waterleo-road. On that day Hampstead Races were being run. On the 2ed June witness went to the same place at noon and saw defendant standing there. Three men want to defendant who pulled a newspaper out of his pocket. They looked at It and afterwar Is went away. Some- thing passed from the defendant to ths man but he could not tell what it was. On the 3rd June witness went there at 11.55. At noon three men gave him slips of paper ; at 12.15 tivelmen ; at 12.21 two men. The races on that day were at Upson On Friday the 6th June witness arrived at 11 m. Defendant was then standing in Lowlands-road. Two men accosted him, one of whom gave defendant a slip. De- fendant then gave the man something from his pocket. At 11.35 witness went to Percival-lane. At 11.45 three men gave defendant slips; at 12.5 three men ; at 12.20 one man ; at 12.25 one man ;

at 12.35 witness went along the road and the defendant walked away ov rr Waterloo Bridge. On Saturday the 7th at 11.15 p.m.. he Saw him ire Shaw-street in company with Constable Edwards, Witness told defendant what he had seen, and asked him s to accompany him to the police station. On being searched several pocket books relating to bets were found in his possession, also a statement of money received and money owing.—For the defence it was contended that the defendaat had never been cautioned by the police, or he would have discontinued frequenting the place.—Defendant was fined 40s and costs.

div.head: Forming the Divisions,
div.p: Forming the Divisions,
Brighouse Rangers Re-admitted in the First Flight,

A protracted meeting of the Northern League was held on Tuesday afternoon and evening at . the George Hotel, Huddersfield, under the presidency of Mr J Clifford (Huddersfield). The transfer of H Hadwen, Morecambe to Halifax wee granted.

It was resolved that the Brighouse Rangers club be re- admitted to the First Division of the Northern League. The following applications to go in the Seoond Division of the League were granted T.-York, South Shields, Widnes, =loss, Castieford, Halbeck, Bromley, Rochdale Hornets. Morecambe, Keighley, Norocanton.Leeds,St Helens. Barrow, Stockport, Wakefield Trinity. Manningham, Dewsbury, Birkenhead, Hull Kingston Revers, and Lancaster. Radcliffe's application was refused. This makes a:membership of 36 clubs for the two Divisions ofjthe League. It was resolved that at the next meeting the whole of the clubs in the League shall vote three clubs from the Second to the First Division, the vote to be by ballot, the whole of the representatives present to have the right to vote, but no vote to be valid unless it affects three clubs,and the vote to be an exhaustive one.
It was decided to seed to each club in membership a copy of tbe rules which are to be considered at the next meeting, to be held in Maachester on the Jet of July.

div.head: GENEROUS GIFT.
div.p: A GENEROUS GIFT.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE " EXAMINER." Sir,—The deep interest taken by his gracious Majesty in our hospitals appears to us to make a Coronation gift of the portraits of their gracious Majesties the King and Queen to these splendid institutions, peculiarly appro. priate, and we have much pleasure in informing you that we have decided to present 1,000 fac-simile oil painting portraits of their Majeaties tha King and Queen, to fiva hundred of the hisoitals of London and the pro- vinces. May we ask you to be good enough to facilitate the presentation by intimating in an early issue of your valuable Journal that the portraits will b 3 al:otted to the respective hospitals in the rotation in which appli- cations from the secretaries reach us. The picturs will be delivered carriage paid, and framed complete. We have the honour to remain, yours faithflilly, RAPHAEL TUCK & SONS, LIMITED.

BEN-lIIIR " AT EIftIIELY-LANE THEA TRE.—Evon those who have seen " Ben-Hur "—and no one should miss this superb spectacular drama—can form only a very vague and approximate estimate of the number of people employed in the presentation of this rernarkatle play, which is drawing all ' London to Drury-lane theatre. Besides an exceptionally large executive staff employed in the conabhsed Anglo-American manage- ment and the list ef principal actors and actresses whose Ealal°s appear on the programme, there is, in addition, a well trained chorus of about 100 male and female voices. and another 100 black and white supers, who, with all the stage-ban de, scene-shifters, machinists, arpenters, horsemen, k incidentally employed in this tupendous production, combine in making a grand total of no less than six hundred. Many Wa rringtonians Will be visiting the capital during next week and we should advise them not to:mies the opportunity of nein Ben-Hur."

div.head: Ihe Late Miss Gaskell and Mrs. Sharp.
div.p: Ihe Late Miss Gaskell and Mrs. Sharp.
Pulpit Reference.

- - , Reference was made by the Rev E C E Carletsn Holy Trinity Church on Sunday morning to the death of Miss Gaskell and Mrs Sharp, both members of the con. gregation. He based hie sermon on the text " The hope that is laid up for you in heaven." Those who knew Miss Gasket!, he said, best know what the loss is to us all. There are many here who mourn the loss of a sincere and genuine friend and benefactor. How far her kindnesses went none of us can tell, for they were never obtruded ; not were they carelessly or randomly bestowed. They were evir the dictate of ptudence, and of kindly thought as well as of generos- ity. Is it any wonder that she went about with ths,'s happy smile which won our hearts—the index of a mind at peace with itself and delighted in the well-being of others ? And what shall we say of our dear friend Mrs Sharp, who, though less intimate)" known to the oulk of the congregation, owing ti her health obliging her to live much ill retirement. was none the leas a warm and generous friend of Chill church. While we mourn her loss on her own account. I think also many here will feel melancholy in recalling the fact that she is tha last in this locality to bear 15 nam• that must ever be venerable in the town of War- rington—a name which it is our pride to remember wa. for many years ideatified with this church. The nanse of Sharp, I fear, will now pass away, as far as we are cancernsa, from the records of Trinity Courch. It is liks entering en a new phase of parochial history. Let us trust God will raise up others lik3 them in the future.

div.head: NASAL CATARRH-SYMPTOMS AND TREATMENT.
div.p: NASAL CATARRH-SYMPTOMS AND TREATMENT.

Catarrh of the Nose is usually the result of a neg- lected colder of a succession of colds, in fact, manY people who have this disease believe that they are only suffering from an obstinate cold in the head. With chronic catarrh the symptoms of an ordinary cold az* constantly present, the accumulations of mucus in moo and threat and the difficulty in breathing through th 6 nostrils usually constituting the most annoying eymp- touts. But the catarrhal disease does not stop here ; A is always ageeeeeive, always ready to extend from the head to the throat, to the ears, to the lungs, to the stomach, and finally to effect the whole ayetens h 9 absorption of the poisonous discharges into the blood. With these dangers always threatening catarrhal sufferers, it is unfortunate that the disease is believed t? be incurable except by operation. The proof that thit ' view is quite wrong is found in the reports of mired cases published by the Drouet Institute, which include many Instances where a cure was effected by a simple method after operations had boon performed without success.

Those who desire to know the treatment prescribed ,1 at the Institute can obtain full particulars from " The Journal for :the 'Deaf," an Analytical Review of the Diseases of the Ear, Nose, and Throat, which is sent free by post to anyone addressing the Secretary, Drouat Institute, Regent's Park-road, London, N.W. With tbe " Journal "is always enclosed a "Supplement," con- taining details of the cases cured during each month, and also a Patient's Report Form, which enables anyone ta receive free advice as to tho application of the treat` runt at home. Those who desire to hava the ears, nose and throat examined by a specialist are reminded tho they can take advantaas of the reduced railway faree at Corocatios time and visit the Drotiq Ineltute. The fee for examination will remain, as usual, 53 during the, regular consultation hours, 2 to 4 p.m. week days, bals those who may wish to be examined at soma other hour of the day can arrange for a special consultation by writing to the Secretary, De-met Institute, R.gect.'4 Park-road, Primrose-hill, Landon. The Institute Wi b 3 closed June 26:h and 27ch.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

Mishap to a Picnics Party. The members of the Wycliffe Church Choir had an, unusual experience on Saturday on the occasion a their annual picnic when a visit was paid to OPP ancient and interesting city of Chester. The partY which had at its head the organist,Mr W H Payton Must Bac , and Mr R H Pearson, numbered 24 AL' told. They entrained in a special saloon which left Bank Quay Station at 2-40 p.m., and on arriving 10 Chester wended their way to the river for the put pose of boarding an electric launch, which was t° convey them to Farndon. They had only proceeded a short distance up the river when, to use the words of one of the passengers. "something werA wrong with the electric motor," impeding the pro- gress of the boat. However, the defect was suffi- ciently remedied to enable the launch to proceed I slowly to Farndon where a substantial tea was pre" vided for the party by Mrs McCready, who WO formerly manageress of the White Hart Hotel, Market-place. After a rest and a ramble in thie charming part of Cheshire, a start was made for home, as the party were anxious to reach Chester in time to catch the 10 p.m. train. On the return journey, however, there was another mishap with the electric motor " the works went wrong," and after repeated attempts to get the launch aloegt all of which ended in a dismal failure, it wet; determined to make for land. The launch wate got to the bank and the party walked across Ole fields in search of the nearest house where thel could obtain information as to their whereabouts. To their surprise they found they were at Poulton, seven miles from the station, at 9 p.m.. and no con- veyance of any kind to be had I One can twill imagine the Chagrin and disappointment of the visitors, especially of the ladies. A conference vrss bell, and it was decided to proceed to the station on foot. Chance brought the party to a telegracoll office, where messages were despatched to friends at Warrington informing them of the accident,thile allaying the alarm which would otherwise have been felt at the non arrival of the party at the tittle expected, viz., at 10.45, Chester station was not reached until 11 o'clock, and when the facts of the case were reported to one of the railway officials, private.room was placed at the disposal of the un- fortunate pleasure seekers, and here the time was spent, pleasantly on the whole until the first train left on Sunday morning at 2.32. To the surprise of many members of the congregation who bad heard of the choir's experience, there was a fairlY ergs choir at the morning service.

LOCAL WEDDINGS.

Gidman—McLarty. The marriage of Mr F Gidrnan, of Padgate, and Miss Mc',arty, of Egerton-street, was solemnized at St, John's Presbyterian Church, Winwick-street, on Thursday last week. The officiating minister was the Rev J L Milne, and the ceremony was witnessed by a large congregation. Tin bride was handsomely attired in a white silk dress, prettily tucked and trimmed with cbiffjn passementerie and lace, with white chiffon and lace hat to match. She carried s choice shower bouquet. Miss Smallwood and Miss Hope were the two bridemalde,and they wore dresses ef a pale shade of grey voile, trimmed with lsce applique and crepe de chine, with black picture hats. They also carried beautiful bouquets and ware pearl and turquoise brooches, the gift of the bridegroom. The duties of best man were faithfully discharged by Mr James Sullen. A reception was held at the house of the bride's sister, Mrs Clayton, of Manchester-road. The honeymoon is being spent at Llangollen and Barmouth. The following is a list of presents : Bridegroom to Bride, pearl brooch Bride to Bridegroom, signet ring Mrs RlcLarty, household linen, china &cc. Mrs Gidman, piano and music cabinet Mr McLarty, coal cabinet and cheque Miss Smallwood, silver cruet Miss Hope, silver cake basket Mr J Millen, china tea service Mr and Mrs Mann, brass standard lamp Master Reggie Mann, upholstered foot stool Mr and Mrs H Clayton. Lounge chair Mr W Humphreys, toilet service Miss Allen, brass:and copper mirror Miss Barlow. silver salts Mrs Bennett, toilet mats Mr and Mrs Bowen, coal box Mr William Clarke. Chippendale table Mr and Mrs Box, silver and pearl cake knife Mr and Mrs Bradley,copper spirit kettle and stand Mr and Mrs R Chaloner, silver sugar sifter Mr E Coates, silver cigarette case Mrs Davies, 5 o'clock tea stand Mrs Davies (Howley), ornament and household utensils Mr and Mrs T:Fryer Evans, sliver feru vase Mr and Mrs Harrington, table cloth Mr Hodgkinson, silver tea service Mr A Hodgkinson, silver match box Staff, W Hodgkinson, Ltd., silver fruit stand Mrs and Miss Hodgkinson, silver hot water jug Miss Jeffrey and Mr Pretty, silver fruit and lower stand Mr and Mrs Lunt, silver sugar bowl and sifter Mrs Mason, afternoon tea set Mr and Mrs Massey, silver salts Mrs Mitchell. table cover Mr and Mrs It Molyneax, silver photo frame Mr F Morris, album Mr B Morris, iron and capper cake stand Miss S Morris, copper crumb tray and brush Mr and Mrs Phillips, pair placques Mr J Smallwood. china placque Mr and Mrs G Sutton, silver inkstand Miss Tastier, silver toast rack Mr and Mrs D E Watson, hand painted panel Mr and Mrs PT Winskill, bracket and mirror Mrs Bioletti, tea cosy Storey—Daintith. _ . . . .

- . At Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Thursday last week, the marriage took place of Mr J B Storey, of Manchester-road and Miss Nellie Daintith, daughter of Mr Thomas D tintitb, of Wilderspool Causeway, who has carried on the business of a gunsmith in Bridge- street fer many years. The ceremony was witnessed by a large .congregation. Daring the arrival of the wedd- ing guests several appropriate voluntaries were played on the organ by Mr George Weaver The bride, who was given away by her lather, looked pretty in a dress of French grey, trimmed with white crepe-de-chine and'Honiton peint lace. She also wore a white crinoline hat with large white plumes and carried a shower bouquet of white roses and lilies of the valley. The bridesmaids were Miss Storey (sister of the bride- groom) and Miss Beatrice Daintith (cousin of the bride. They wore grey dresses, trimmed with white silk. Their bouquets were composed of marguerites and they wore gold bangles,' he gift of the bridegroom. The duties of best man were satisfactorily performed by Mr Bert. Diiutith. Duriree the service, the hymn " The Voice that breathed o'er Elen " was sung and at the close, the organist played Mendelssolen's " Wedding March." The Rev Theodore Bishop was the officiat- iag minister. Luncheon was afterwards served at the house of the bride's father. The newly-married couple departed later in the day for Pen- maeumawr. They dwere the recipients of many choice presents, including several from the members of the staff of Messrs Summers, of Manchester, by which firm the bridegroom is employed.

div.head: Darlington—Beech.
div.p: Darlington—Beech.

The marriage was solemnized at Daresbury on Thurs. day,last week of Miss Hannah Horton Darlington, eldest daughter of Mr Thomas Darlington, Daresbury, and Mr Herbert Beech, of Plumbley. A large congregation attended the service, which was fully choral. The officiating clergymen were the Vicar (Rev F Clifton Smith) and the Bev E B May. The bride looked charm- ing in a dress of white silk, trimmed with embroidered lace. She wore a wreath of °rang* blossom,and carried a handsome bouquet cf roses,the gift of the bridegroom The bridesmaids were Miss A Darlington, and Miss ha Darlington (sisters of the bride) and Miss Beech (sister of the bridegroom). div.head: Back to South Africa.
div.p: Back to South Africa.

At two o'clock on Monday afternoon a good number of ladies and gentlemen, friends of Mr Her- bert Erskine (son-in-law of Mr David Fanshaw, of Stafford-road, Stockton Heath, manager of the Whitecross Works),assembled at Bank Quay Station, for the purpoee of seeing him start on his joorney to London en route to South Africa. He left by the 2.5 train, a cheer being raised as the train steamed out of the platform. It may be interesting to note that Mr Erskine is returning to Johannesburg to resume the position held by him before the out- break of the war when he was engaged at the Bonanza mines,which are situated at Johannesburg. When war was declared Mr Erskine joined Bethune's mounted infantry corps, and passed through several engagements, and after serving 14 months was invalided home in February, 1901, where he has since remained,having been employed at Warrington as draughtsman and engineer at the Whitecross Works. He sailed on Tuesday from Southampton in the steamship Staffordshire. Warrington P.S.A. Society.

The soloist was Mr Cotterill, whose singing was thoroughly enjoyed. The Scripture lesson was read by Mr W Barnes, and the pray or was offered by Mr Beckett. In the avoidable absence of the Rev Charles Finch, Mr Light was the speaker, and he gave an excellent address on "Sowing and reap- ing." A. " brief, bright and brotherly service was concluded with the Benediction.

div.head: Mr. JohnjMorley.as a Politician.
div.p: Mr. JohnjMorley.as a Politician.

_ s—lt was with ereat pleasure that I read your leading article in your last issue, on Mr Morley's speech at Edinburgh. The " Examiner " appears to b 3 the only paper localy which considers it worth its while to notice editorially any public utterance of Mr Merlee'a On the political sitcatien. By your contemporaries, I pre iume, he is regarded as an effete politician whose , opinions are of no account ia the light of the new Gospel of Imperialism but who is tolerated merely for his ' literary attainmeats which, even they are compelled t admit, entitle him to a respectful hearing ; but to take him seriously as a politician they decline—on principle —or for lack of it. This—it seems to me—is the spirit which actuates most of the Tory and Unionist newspapers in their treat- ment of him. Many ignore him entirely, except when they can cite some portion of his speeches or writings to : illustrate points which they imagine may tell against the party of which he is the most trusted leader. Others harp on the non-fulfilment of many of his prophecies which they characterize as" Cassandra-like," and aver that he bits lost credit as a prophet irretrievably. Time will show ; meanwhile it will be well for those who have treated tie predictions contemptuously hither- to to refrain from hasty jubilation on their failure. The " Examiner " 1 am glad to find stands above tbis , Sort of thing. It recognizes in Mr Morley a true inheritor of the spirit which enimated-thosegreat men who fought so nobly in the past, and spent their lives in the public service to the incalculable advantage of their country- men, and for the principles which they held to be so absolutely necessary to the welfare—not only of the people of this great Empire , but of the world at large —and which he holds and preaches in these days when the very name of Liberate= seems to have fallen into disfavour. It recognizes in him one whose patriotism is not the kiud which says that if you believe your country to be turning down a wrong path —even if that path leads to destruction—you must not offer your advice. You must not raise a warning voice—because • it would be unpatriotic, or disagree with the actions of the Government of the day. To endure torrents of abuse and obloquy such as have been prured on Mr Morley and his friends, requires eurteiotesvz indeed: it is not an easy matter to face a meet- ing,as MeMorley did in September 1899 at Manchester.to protest aeainst the spirit in which public negotiations were being conducted with anoteer country by Ministers of the Crown when the meeting is composed mainly of people eagerly wishing for war. To do such a thing re- quires a courage which is not born of Jingoism, but which is the result of moral rectitude and the knowledge that one has taken infinite pains to ascertain the truth about the matter and is convinced that he is in the right. It requires, in addition, a patriotism of the very noblest type and John Morley possesses in no mean degree, both of these essential qualities. Mr Morley is a man whom the Liberal party could ill afford to lose. Ingrained in him is that passionate love of truth and justice which burnt so intensely in the breast of John Stuart Mill. He possesses that noble fearlessness which So distinguished John Bright. His Intimate companion- ship with Mr aladstone, Mr Gladstone's fervid love for him and Mr Morley 'a acceptance of his principles of policy mark him out as the chief representative of Gladstouian Liberalism in England. No member of arlisment occupies a more honoured place in the Councils of the Liberal party. The Liberal Party is not by any means in the majority nor is it as progressive as we could wish. During the last 20 years the death of many great men ta3 dealt so heavy a blow to the Party that it is necessary to make greater claims on those who remain. It needs men whose sovereign aim is to promote the advancement of the people of this country and who are prepared to make any sacrifice to further that end ; and it has a magnificent example in Mr John Morley I—Yours faithfully, 18th June, 1902.
A RADIC

ATHLETIC SPORTS AT EARLESTOWN. In connection with St John's Men's Bible Class, th. first Annual Amateur Athletic Festival was held on th. ground of the Earlestown Football Club,on Saturday afternoon. The weather was somewhat threatening in the morning, but as the day advanced it cleared off,and althought it was rather cool, the day was otherwise propitious, and the large crowd of spectators bad the pleasure of witt essing some good sport. The Earlestown Prize Band was present, and during the afternoon dis- coursed some excellent and enlivening music: There were nearly 250 entries for the various events including competitors from the surrounding towns. The judges were Dr Mouncey, Rev Father O'Reilly, Messrs A Brown, J Singleton, R Chandley, and A F Golden. Starter, Mr John Rylance ; referee, Mr L E Pilkington ; marksmen, Messrs W Johnson,T Ellis, I Boon, J Sharpe, A J Johnson, J Ellison, H Sheridan and E Davies. TEACHERS AND CORPORAL PUNISHMENT.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday morning, Mr George Faulkner. bead master of St Mary's Catholic School, was charged with assaulting and beating a boy named Martin M'Quirk, on Friday last. Mr Knowles defended, Michael M'Quirk said that on the noon of Friday he came home from work and saw his son lying apparently ill on the sofa. The boy complained of severe punishment while at school. Upon examin- ation, marks were found upon his sb,oulders. Wit nese took him to Inspector Strickland, who saw the marks. The boy made a long statement, in which he alleged his master had thrashed and kicked him right and left.' Inspector Strickland; gave evidence as to the marks, but, in his opinion, none had been caused by kicks. Thomas Quinn, twelve yeArs of age, said he was in school when Martin M'Quirk came in late. According to custom, late corners are caned. As soon as M'Quirk had been caned he made for the door to go home. lie was brought back and struck on the seat three times. The bench retired for a few minutes, and then Stated that they had come to the conclu,sion that the punishment inflicted was entirely done with a cane. The case would be dismissed, but they would recommend that greater care should be taken in the infliction or corporal punishment upon the boys

div.head: L&TCEIFORD.
div.p: L&TCEIFORD.

It is evident that the festivities at Latchford will be quite worthy of the great event. Tne arrangements which have been made by the committee were Drought before the inhabitant+ at a public meeting held in the Parish Room on Tuesday evening. The Vicar (Rev F A Bcreeton) presided over a good attendance. The Chairman said he had to announce some news which he thought they would all welcome, and that was that the collectors had been successful in raising over £4O. tie understood there VV,IB more money to come in, and he had to than the collectrns for the energy they had displayed Too committee wished to express their names to Mr Hewitt vvh had very kindly placed a field at their disposal. Perhaps some of those present were aware that Mr Ashley, of Wash-lane, had already offered a field, and Mr Johnson hal offered the use of 9 shed, but although the committee were for various reasons, not in a position to accept these off3rs, they publicly expressed their thanks for them. It had been arranged that all the children of Latchford should be entertained to tea in the Parish Room on Coronation Day, commencing at tour o'clock. They would also have a tea on the following day. The old people of the parish would be entertained in the Temperance Hall by the kind permission of Counc'llor Luke Elko% Toe tender of Mr Horton for catering had been accepted. There wete to b 3 a great many sports during the afternoon aud evening, includ- ing a tug of war, in which teams selectectfrom local works would compete, The Committee would be glad to have the assistance of ladies to preside over the tables at the children's tea. It was proposed to commence the celebrations by a public proce.ssioa from the Wash- lane school, the headquarters of the band, to the field. Tine procession will at art at two o'clock, and the inhabi- tants are invited to take part in it. In the evening the rejoicings would wind up with Na torchlight procession, , in Which there would be two hundred torches. He hoped they would all work together, and make the fes- tivities a great success. The Coronation was a national event in which every person in the parish ought to be interested.—A. sub-committee was then appointed to make arraneements for the sport.—On the motion of Councillor Elinor], the Vicar was Clrdiany thanked for presiding, and the meeting concluded.

Full Arrangements for the Town's an Friendly Societies' Procession.

The programme of the arrangements for the Town's and Friendly Societies' procession in Coron- ation Day has now been issued. Tile procession will fall in at the Town Hall Grounds in the fol- lowing order, in formation of four deep, under the direction of the Town's Marshal (Mr Luke Talbot, Chief Constable) :- 1 Detachment of Police.

2 Volunteer Band and Battalion. 3 Ambulance Brigade. 4 Fire Brigade. 5 Clergyman of all Denominations. 6 Tne Mayor, Mayoral Suite, and Borough Member. 7 Freemen of the Borough. 8 Aldermen, Councillors, and Justices of the Borough. 0 Principal Corporation Officials. 10 Guardians of the Poor and Rural District Councillors. 11 Friendly Societies (in the order shown in the accompanying table). . .

For convenience of expression in this programme the above-mentioned bodies,from number 1 to num- ber 10,will be referred to as section 1 of the proces- sion. Number 11 (Friendly Societies) will;be called section number 2.

At 10 a.m. the Marshal's bugler will sound the ,g Assembly," and section number 1 of the proces- sion should at once form four deep in the drives of the Town Hall, the Volunteer band and battalion taking up their position in the east drive with their band and head of column resting on the centre gate. The remainder of section 1 will fall in behind the battalion, in proper sequence, up the east drive and so on round the whole of the walk,'the rear of section 1 being nearest to the west gate. Section number 2 will occupy the lawn. Entering the Park br;the centre gate (as per Time Table) the first Society (Ancient Order of Rechabites) will pass up the lawn to the side nearest Bath-street, and halt at the top facing the Town Hall, and the other Societies will form beside it in rotation. Their waggons are to be drawn up in proper numer- ical order in Bath-street and Legh-streer. ready to enter the Town Hall grounds by Bath-street entrance and fall in behind their respective Socie- ties when directed by the police. The first waggon should be resting on the Bath-street entrance. No horsed vehicles other than these (and such private carriages as may be authorised by his Worship the IMayor ; will be allowed inside the Town Hall grounds, or to take part in the procession. At 10 3f) when the Procession should be ready to start, the bugler will sound the "Advance." The whole of the processioniste should then face the Town Hall steps, where the Mayoress will wave the National Flag. At this signal the Volunteer Band I will play one verse of the National Anthem, which the processioniste are respectfully requested to sing in unison with the band. At the close of this ceremony the procession will immediately move off upon its route, leaving the grounds by the centre gate. The Friendly societies will pass down the West drive and out at the centre gate. Having traversed the route all will return to the Town Hall grounds, section number 1 going in by uhe west gate and taking up its position in the drives exactly as before the start. Section number 2 will re-enter by the centre gate and take up the same posiOon on the lawn as before the start. All will stand fast (in position as before the start) until a signal is given by bugle-call, when all will face the Town Hall and a second verse of the National

Anthem will be played and sung as before. The procession will then disperse. When the societies are re-entering the grounds alter traversing the route their waggons will go down Arpley-street and U 2 Winrnarleigh-street, at the top of which latter street No 1 waggon will stand, the others falling in behind it, and all the vehicles will wait tu join their respective societies after the dispersal of the Procession.
_Friendly Societies will leave the grounds as follows :

1 (Ftechabites), Wrinmarleigh-street, Museum- street, St Austin's-lane. 2 (Free Gardeners), an key-street, llorse- market-street. 3 (Druids), Springfield-street, Palmyra-square. 4 (National Order of Oddfellows), Sankey- street, Legh-street, Bath-street. 5 (Manchester Unity Oddfellowsl, Sankey- street, Bold-street. 6 (Forresters), sankey-street, Golborne-street. 7 (Grand United Odd fellows), Straight across to Conservative Club. 8 (Ancient Order of Shepherds),Sankey-street, Legh-street, Edgeworth-street, Bewsey- street, and Be wsey-roaa 9 (Butchers), Sankey-street, Corporation- street. GENERAL DIRECTIONS TO TIIE FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

Each society must be at its point of rendezvous strictly to time, neither before nor after, and reach it by the route laid down in this programme. Each society must carry throughout the whole proceed- ings, conspicuously displayed at its head, a stall and number-card corresponding with its numerical order in the Friendly Societies' Section

- of the procession. Each waggon must have a similar staff and card properly displayed. No Society to move from its point until called up by the police, who will deal with Head Marshals only. Each Head Marshal is to hold the staff and card of his Society at the point of rendezvous. kll waggons to be in Bath-street and Legh-street not later than 9.30 a.m. Mounted Marshals may enter the park but should at once remove their horses should the animals become restive or dangerous. The last (Butchers') Society, consisting entirely of mounted men, will be called from the top of Bold. street by the police and taken into the recreation ground by the west gate of that ground. They will there form four deep in such a manner that the first four of the column will rest just inside the gateway whicti divides the recreation ground from the Town Hall drives. When their turn comes they will ride through this gate and torm the "mounted screen" at the rear of the procession. Whe? the piocession returns to the Town Hall the mot/Wed butchers will not re-enter the grounds but wit' ride straight down Parker-street and go to their des- tination. Staffs and number cards will be supplied by the Chief Constable, to whom all communica- tions connected with the organisation of the pro- cession should now be addressed.

The following is the route of the procession : West Drive, Sankey-street, Bridge-street, Morse- street. Church-street (right hand side), round the big lamp in Cnurch Place, back down Churcb- street, Irlam-street, Buttermaket-street, Horse- market-street, Win wick street, Tanners-lane, Cros- field-street, to Town Hall grounds.
