div.head: Chief Constable's "Homely Hints." Chief Constable's Office, Warrington, Jcne_lBtb, 1902, . .
div.p: The Chief Constable's "Homely Hints." Chief Constable's Office, Warrington, Jcne_lBtb, 1902, . .

Sir,—During the past seven years I hay' e often watched with surprise and admiration the conduct of our townspeople when large crowds have been drawn together by public functions and demonstrations. Not- withstanding the :act that many such occasions have been atteLdsj with intense general excitement, tract- ability an wood humour have invariably been marked features ot6these popular assembles in Warrington. Comparing this with my long and varied experience elsewnere, I repeat that at nest I wondered, and from first t 51 I have admired. I have always found the Warriugt ni people ready to tall in with a reasonable r.quest or a comman seose reguiatioo ; they are prompt to see, appreciate, and accept a suggestion for the com- mon good. Tiaey like it to be told them pleasantly but above all they want it to be told plaizay. I ant there- fore encouraged to solicit throueh Oa the favourable coosidera:ion of my fellow towns-folic of toe few homely aud wholesome hints which follow in the hope that our coming Coroottipn celebrations may thereby go more smoothly and leave behold them none but pleasant mernor:es I purposAy avoid the et ltei phrasology ot the statute or bylaw. Tbs is an appeal to the common souse mud good feeling of my te lo v rown'6-folk, a friendly word, in a friendly:way, nog an offi.:ial code or a set of regulations. (1) Oa trio respective routes of the processions fixed decorations across the roadways should not be lower than twenty fee: ; flags and screamers should not hang over the roadway lower Chars sixteen feet. Decorations and iilutninations should not b 3 of a character likely co startleamervous horses.

(2) Spectators, plea>e keep on the side-walks, the roadway; are natrow, anl the prooessionists .viil march four deep ; don't congregit; at any one point so as to crngest it. Yu wifl 8,9 the preeesnion equally well at any place along the line of route. (5) Parents and frieilds, kindly leave your children alone when they are marching, don't walk along side of them or otherwise interfere, they 'ailt be all right. (4) Grown up people, peqtect the little ones ; men, please help the police when necessary to control horse traffic where it mi4at be dangerous to life or limb.

(5) Please don't push or jostle in the crowds, consider the ladies and the little ones, give them the front places as vuu almost always do. (6) In case of serious aceldent, call the nearest Cen- stabie ; the Warringten police are all ambulance .neo. A telephone message to the Central Police Station (No. 74) will bring the horse ambulance in a few minutes to any part of cue to we. Use the nearest available tele- phole. The police stations at Latchford,Saukey Bridges, ' and Winwick-road have telephonic communications. (7) In case of electric wires falling into tee streets keep of them lithely are not in contact with any living thing. Samna' n the police or call up the Electrical De- partment on ti.e telephone (No. 206). If the wires must j he touched they should be touched with hands pro:ected b 7 rubber. A good big rubber tobacco pouch makes a j god hand guard. J (8) Prefessional t`iieves look upon public celebrations J as a harvest time. Don't leave your hou,es altogether unoccupied either night or day if you can help it. If you must leave them so, secure all wiodows, doors, gates aud grid. Carefully conceal and remove valuables to a place ef safety. A misy deg in a la)use is the best " scare-thief "I keow. Sioiu d you be going away and leaving your houses without a ayone in cearge over night send inn a lice to say so and the police will give your premises such special atteetion that you need not worry about them. This applies all the year round. (9) Beware of nickplekets. Hotel-keepers and pub- Beaus, look out for the professional thief woe invadee your bedrooms and other private apartments in search of plunder just at your busiest time. His confederates sometimes organise a uisturb ince in tee /sense whilst their partner is at work to distract the landlord's atten- tion, and the latter may lose his watch and guard in the process of ejecting them. If you notice anything sus- picious, let the p)lice know quickly and quietly. (10) Bands whilst passing places of worship during divine service should cease playing. Tnis lam pleased to say is usually observed in Warrington.

(1.1) Fellow townsmen generally, help your servants the police all you can at this trying time. (12) Please do' t make unnecessary noises in the streei s after midnight. Remember the sick and the bed-ridden who need sleep. They will have no part ia the r joicings but at least we can give them peace at night. (13) The Official Programme signed by His Worship the Mayor nod oircu!atel by ca,', contains the correct and authorised version of the times, routes, Ana general arrangements for both processions. I fear, dear Mr Etlitor,l have trespassed terribly upon your space but it will be a long time before we have another Coronation (I sincerely trust) and I do not often indul;e in newspap,r correspondence. I enclosa you a copy of the Official Progrimado for the Town's and Friendly S)cieties Procession on Thursdly June 26 t inst. _

Speech by Mr. A. H. Crosfield.

Thera was an encouraging attendance at the annual meeting of the General Council of the War- rington Liberal Association, held in the Liberal Club, Be wsey-streec, on Wednesday evening. Mr. Councillor Tinnion was voted to the chair, and there were also present :—,fir A H Crosfield, Councillors Ellison, James Evans, T Barton, Peacock, Malkin, Wilkinson; Messrs James Dodds, John Harrison, William Furness, C Jackson Holmes, J Bailey, Thomas Pemberton, J Critchley, Mitchell, Dixon, Hayward, Willett, Crosskill, Cooke, Shaw, Wright, Hewitt, Locker, Hughes, A Downes ,Pritchard, and others.

LETTERS OF APOLOGY. Too CHAIRMA.N read a comaiunication from Coun- cillor F R Roberts regretting his inability to be pre- sent. " Toe party," Councillor Roberts continued, " can always count on my services—such as they are. adacation bills and bread taxes are enough to make one wonder whether the old Toryism was not better than the new Unionism. At all•events it was more straightforward I believe Liberalism will have the best chance at the next election than it has had since 1835. Locally, we shall be very much to blame if we do not give a good account of our- selves."

_ Councillor William Pierpoint, writing from the Natioual Liberal Club, iiihitehall Place, London, S.W., said :—" lam sorry that 1 cannot baa 7. the meeting to-night of the association, a prior engage- ment here prevents ma. I am in thelfullest sym- pathy with my party and intend using whatever influence I may possess to further its progress in Warrington. I hope the meeting will elect Mr Ziba Armitage to fill the position so worthily held by the late Mr John Crosfield and to whom the Liberal party owes sO mach." Mr E J Guest wrote to Mr Tinniou :—" lam much obliged for your favour of the lfich inst and would have made an effort to be at the meeting of the Liberal Association but unfortunately am cir- cuit steward of the Frodshana circuit and the cparterly meeting is fixed for the 18th inst. As you are aware I am opposed to the Education Bill because it is framed in the interests of sectarian- ism and will tend to hinder a true system of national education. The corn tax is, I fear, not designed simply to secure additional revenue; but is an attempt to bring back protec- tion and to help forward tile scheme of Zollverein which has SO much favour in the eyes of Mr Chamberlain. Favoured treatment to our colonies can only be secdred by imposing tariff on goods imported from foreign countries, and as our trade with our colonies is not more than one-fourth of the whole it would be suicidal to injure three- fourths of our trade in order to please our colonies much as we wish to hind them more ciosely to us. 'Free Trade is an absolute necessity for this coLn- try. We rejoice exceedingly in the restoration of peace in South Africa and look forward to the development of this extension of his Majesty's dominions with great hope. The principles of Liberalism alone can put our colonies on right lines Both at home and abroad we need the Liberal party back in power in the interests of progress, liberty and economy. With Rosebery as prime-minister and Campbell Bannermann as leader of the House of Commons backed by Harcourt, Asquith, Fowler, Morley, Perks, fAloyd-Greorge, Fletcher, Moulton we should have one of the strongest govern- manta of modern times. But to put them in power will mean that Liberals of all shades of opinion shall work together for the common good. Prin- ciples must be faced and then fought for. Locally our onlv hope is this. Too much I fear we have trimmed and gone along the line of least resistence, Expediency rather than unflinching devotion tto duty has actuated us. Hence there has been no enthusiasin,the electors seeing very little to choose between one party and the other. What we want is convictions.
Mr O'Bnuor chairman of the Town Halt Ward Committee also wrote expressing his regret at being nable to be present. MR. CRO6NIELD PROPOSES A RESOLUTION. INURES TING SPEECH.

Mr. a.. IL CnosFIELD, who on riming to- speak received a hearty reception, moved the following ro,olution " That this meeting rejoices in the restoration of peace in South Africa, and Looks forward Co the developinenr of this exterusion of Hie Majeity'S I.IOIIIiIUXIS With great hope ; that this meeting earnestly protests against tide Education Bill now °gore Parliament, believing it to be educationally unseund and denominationally unjust ; and further condemns the bread tax as a retrograde policy." He said : I think that as this is the first neeete log we have had since the conclusien of the war, it is not unfitting that we should give expression to the feel- iug of thankfulness that must be in the minds of every thoughtful citizen in this tow,' and of this country. (Rear, hear.) The shadow of black death, which like a peetilence of the old days in this country, has been spread abroad in those large traets of country in South Africa, has been dissipated. About the question which precsded the war there have been in this town,as elsewhere in England, some differences of opinion— (hear, hear)—but in the thankfulness with which we recognise the conclueion of the war there is no die?erence of opinion. (Hear, hear.) Neither is there any differ- ence of opinion in the feelings we entertain towards the British soldiers who faced the long strain of' this arduous battle in South Arrice. (Hear, heir.) As regards our Soldiers one scarcely knows whether to admire more the indomitable courage and the dash which they showed in their engagements or the patient fortitude with which they faced mouth alter month all that dreary and monotonous life involved in what has been called the blockhouse system. (Hear, hear.) Then as regards the great soldier upon whese shoulders devolved the chief responsibility for carrying our opera- tions in the field to a successful issue. I am sure you eel, as I feel, a deeper and deeper admiraticn and respect, not alone for the capacity for organisation, for :the tireless energy, for the soldier-like skill, but I must add for the true magnanimity that bespeaks the statesmen, for the foresight and brad-mindedness which Lord Kitchener has displayed. (Applause.) I daresay you were struck by a passage in a very fice speech which Mr Morley made the other day in Edin- burgh. He referred to the touching and striking scene at Vereeniging when Lord Kitchener met the Boer dele- gates, and when he is reported to have said that if he had been in their place he would have been proud to do what they had done. Mr Morley well said he would have voted L-rd liit,abener £50,000 fer that remark alone. (Cheers.) There are many of Us here who have condemned, and who who still condemn the reckless and overbearing kind of diplomacy which throughout the summer of 1899 made war almost inevitable. Mr Chamberlain told the Governor of Natal at that time that during four months of negotiations we had obtained eine-tentbs of what we stipulated for at the outset and there are 40831 Of us;who think, as Sir Edward Clarke told Mr Chamberlain face to face in the House of Commons that the other one- tenth was never worth all this vast expenditure ot blood and treasure and the iocalculah!e misery Yvbic has been ceneed in South Africa. (Hear, hear.) In the course of the war we as Liberals have also from time to three strongly condemned what has been said about unconditional aurrmder—(hear, bear)—and I think the settlement that Las been arrived at justifies entirely the position we took up on the matter. (Hear, hear.) So much far the past. Then if you Come to the present time you have Cape Colony, which, is certainly a difficult problem before us. Three years ago Cape Colony was one of the most loyal parts of the whole empire. I know a good deal of it because I am broue,ht in teuoh in business with those who spend their lives in that part of the, empire and I am told that in no part of the whole empire would you have found the Queen's portrait in so many humble cottages as you would have found throughout the Dutch population of Cape Colony. At present we have shaken that feeling of loyalty. We have a difficult problem in front of us but we shall make it worse if we try to pile on the agony by perpetuating the dissolution of the con- stitutional government of Cape Colony. (Hell*, hear.) There is one consequence of the war affecting this country that I would like to allude to and that is the way in which we are almost getting face to face with the demand for Conscription. I think as Liberals we recognise that conscription is opposed entirely to the nature and dispoeition of Englishmen. (Hear, hear.) We are boru individualists and we do our work best, not by force, not by compulsion, but by willing service, (Bear, hear.) Ibis question of con - scription is becerning a pressing one. It concerns the: whole of our forces—the line, the militia, and the volun- teers. I take .this opportunity of saying one word upon tbat, because it concerns us here as it concerns employers of [atriar all through the country. I am sorry to say there is in some quarters a disposition on the part of employers of labour t cold-shoulder workingmen who wish to act as volunteers. Volunteers, as you know, have to spend every al!prnative year a week—end in some cases affecting 25 bittalions—a fortnight in camp. Many employers, I bear, are disposed to penalise the men who wish to undertake that patriotic duty. That is a serious matter, because if you have conecripdon it will mean that a year or two will be taken out of men's lives for military training at the very time when they ought to be working to es- tablish their position in life. How much better than conscription is the alternative of allowing the workmen to attend camp for a week or a fortnight ? The en- campment is a healthy thing for them,; healthy change

in their lives, and a good thins in point of discipline. This is an all-important matter tor °eery patdotic citizen who does n wisn to see us driven into the odious system of conscription which obtaios on the con- tinent. Just in passing may I refer to one or two local matters which should specially interest U 3 in this con- nection. If energetic attempts are being made, 83 they are being made, to found a Soldiers' Club in the town, and at Appleton to teach the rising generation to shoot striaight—(laughter)—l hope that all the enthusiasm cf late years will not be allowed to evaporate int, thin air 'and that those who can well aff 3rd to support such in- •stitutions will give them, entirely without distinction of party, the financial assistance and the backing they so well deserve. (Applause). I will only say a word or two on the important matter in our minds just now. Owing to Tory government, national expmditure has gone up at a very serious rate indeed. In the last ten years we have increased our annual ex- penditure at the rate of forty millions, and, of course, you have the little bill to pay. This bread tax has been the Tory solution, I should think all the old Liberals must have rubbsd their eyes when they saw any govern- ment dare to propose a tax like that. I can remember my father and uncle saying to 1119 years ago that never again would an English minister dare to propose to put- a single shilling of taxation upon corn. This Tory' government has done it and as Sir William Harcourt said on the first night it was introduced," You are go- ing to tax the poorest of the poor." The issue is a very simple one for every thoughtful operative to consider. Mr Booth has made it quite clear that a very large pro- portion of our people still are on the brink of extreme want—on the brink of what Mr Booth has called " the submerged teeth." By putting—in so many districts— this extra half-penny a loaf on bread we are going to push a good many over the brink and we are going to diminish the vitality and working capacity and stamina a our labouring population. (Hear, hear.) It is a tax gradated in proportion as people can least afford to pay it. (Hear, hear.) The married man pays more than the single man ; the man with a large family pays more than the man with a small family. In fact it is an epitome of the old Tory policy of taxing labour to relieve property. Apart from the crowded ceetres 'if our great cities, probably there Is no part of the United Kingdom where this tar will operate with more injustice than in the West of Ireland. Our Irish friends in Warrington, or some of them, will have seen,as I have seen, the terrible poverty which has ,to he faced by hundreds of thousands of people oat there in that Western disla•ict, stretching from Donegal southwards, which John Morley once described as "a broad fringe of wretchedness." I don't think a more serious matter could be put before any constituency. People say revenue must be raised somehow. Precisely. We Liberals have got our alternative. (Hear, hear.) Sir Henry Fowler very properly said that the last thing the very last thing you ought to tax is bread. (Hear, hear.) It is not as if there were not plenty of ways of raising money ; and one which we in our party ought to make one of foremost planks in our platform is the taxation of site values. CApplause.) I have referred to this subject more than once, and I have been in com- munication with Mr Celli?, the secretary for the Financial Reform Association, and he has promised to come down here early next autumn and lecture to Us on this important subject.. At previtsus meetings here a good deal has been slid about the absence of education. I can assure you it will not be my fault if the whole question of the taxation of site values is not put fully before the constituency before the end of the year. (Hear, hear.) I may also say that Mr Broadhurst— (applause)—has promised to come down hero if we wish and address us. (Hear, hear.) I have also received letters during tho last few weeks suggesting that we ought to have an ex-Cabinet minister to address us in Warrington. It is for you to say whom you would rather have. I have always been greatly influenced in my political education, and lam to-day influenced,as no doubt many of you are, by the views of that statesman of high integrity, wide experience, and great moral power, John Morley. (Hear, hear, and applause.) I wilt conclude with one word on the education question. It is not necessary to say more because you had the meeting n the Parr Hall and you have no doubt read the speeches of Mr Bryce and Lord Resebery and other competent men on this subject. To my mind it seems to me a deliberate insult to the whole nation that this Tory Government dare at a time like this when we are really beginning to feel the pinch of competition in com- merce as between England and America and England and Germany, where education is more to the fore than in England, that they dare to propose a retrograde measure of this kiud. Lord It osebery summed it up when he said it was calculated to sterilise elueation in ' this country for generations to corn-. (Hear, hear.) It Is a measure, as Mr Parker well put it at the meeting in the Parr Hall. " educationally unsonnd and denomina- tionally unjust." I think if we take steps to bring these , facts home to the constituency, Warrington will realise that there is a differeace—and a very big difference— between Tory legislation and Tory taxation and Liberal methods of dealing with these matters. (Fleas. heesa) That is what we have to do. wa Kaye a splendid ph.lana of ranErats among the working-classes of War- rington. There has been in othsr qaestions a good aeal of apathy in the past and we have got to rem sYe it., (Hear, hear.) I look to the working-classes to take these matters up and help Us to show;the constituency at large that when they were rushed into the last election be special pleading and misleading pretexts they never Wended to let the government upset our.fiscal system or treat us to such legislation as they are now forcing on the country. (Load Applause.)

Liverpool Volunteers from the Front— Arrival at Warrington. The as. Roslin Castle arrived at Smthampton on Wednesday, having on board a number of invalids, officers, and men on their journey home. The list included sixteen officers and men of the Volunt,ser Company Liverpool Regiment (sth Irish), under Lieutenant W G Lindsay; also some men of ;he Lancashire Fusiliers (Lieutenant A B Wigley) and South Lancashire Regiment (Lieutenant-Colonel F A Adam). The Liverpool Volunteers entrained at Southampton for Warrington, and reached their destination on Wednesday night at 9 13. A large number of people witnessed the men's arrival, awi escorted them to Orford Barracks. They were heartily glad that they had arrived so near their Journey's end, for they had hal 4even days march and railway journey frOm Lydenberg to the coast followed by over three weeks' voyage to South- ampton. They looked sunburnt and well, albeit tired of their wearisome railway travel. They lett, Warrington on Thursday afternoon for Liverpool.

WATER POLO. LANCASHIRE COUNTY COMPETITION. WARRINGTON AGAIN DEFEATED. Warrington noir% team met Salford on Tuesday night at the Salford Baths. Salford attacked the deep end. and played a forcing game all through. The brothers Whitehead cent in shot after shot, but were unable to get the tall through. Eventually H Herring receiving a pass from II Whitehead, and gained a goal for Salford. Half-time score :—Stalford, one goal • Warrington. none- Its:the Second half Salford again had the best of the Play, Herring scoring a second point for his team. Result :—Salford, two goals ; Warrington, none. Mr G Jennett was the referee and Mr Whitehead timekeeper.
